speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I wish to move a motion. Unfortunately I was unable to secure the translation into French, and I offer my regrets to the house. It is the first time this has happened to me, but the translation was not returned to me in time. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill):
That the house do now adjourn under standing order No. 26, on a matter of urgent public importance, namely the crisis in international confidence brought about by the speech of the President of the Privy Council on Saturday last in Toronto, which constitutes a public declaration of policy of the gravest national and international significance in that it gives the greatest of encouragement to the communist world and reveals deep enmity toward the policy of the United States administration with regard to the war in Viet Nam, and will result in further and accelerated deterioration in Canada's relations with the U.S.A.; and furthermore, is a travesty on this house which has been denied the enunciation of policy of the government which was made in the said speech outside of this house while parliament is sitting.
May 15, 1967

Speech by President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: SPEECH OF PRIVY COUNCIL PRESIDENT ON VIET NAM-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Will the right hon. Leader of the Opposition address the Chair and the house on the question of urgency of debate? I have at this point to remind hon. members again, as I do from time to time when such motions are made, that what has to be debated before the motion is accepted by the Chair is whether there is urgency of debate in the sense that it is proper for the Chair to grant the adjournment of other business of the house for the purpose of debating a specific question.
This is the only matter which concerns us at the moment, that is the urgency of debate on this particular matter and the advisability of adjourning the ordinary business of the house for the purpose of permitting such a debate.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: SPEECH OF PRIVY COUNCIL PRESIDENT ON VIET NAM-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion is made in order to give the house the opportunity to discuss a matter which is of transcendent importance nationally and internationally, and to secure the views of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, whichever one is directing the foreign affairs of our country.
It might be said immediately that this matter can be discussed in the debate that is now before the house. This is true enough; it can be discussed, but this house has the right to know from the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs what is the government's policy on this question, not the expurgated brush-offs that we have been receiving lately.
Now that the matter has been brought firmly to parliament in the address delivered by the President of the Privy Council I take it that what he enunciated was government policy. To accept any other conclusion in that regard would be to disregard the fixed constitutional principle that cabinet solidarity denies individual ministers the right to enunciate policies. If Your Honour were to say this matter could be dealt with in the debate now before the house, that would in no way clarify the situation. Parliament and the country have the right to know whether the minister was putting forth government policies. The wording of his speech indicates that it was written elsewhere or by those close to the Department of External Affairs. It has all the appearances of having been inspired by the government in order to create a smokescreen in respect of policies of this government. It has all the outward indicia of being a reflection of government policy which this house has not been able to secure.

We have the right to know whether this was a declaration of policy, because no minister can sit in the cabinet and make ad hoc statements on policy contrary to the views of the cabinet, and I must refer to one or two of the statements made in order to found my argument. I wish to read two quotations from that speech, which was delivered to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. At page 2 it reads:
I suppose the answer to these queries-
That is about the world situation in so far as Viet Nam is concerned.
-depends upon our individual consciences-
That statement, sir, is a denial of parliament. Then there is the policy enunciated on page 3:
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
To me it seems that U.S. policy in the Far East has been a succession of unhappy errors beginning with a gross misconception of the weakness and corruption of the Chiang Kai-shek regime in China and then failure to appreciate the relative strength of Mao Tse-tungs* communist government which took power in 1949.
That statement is a slap in the face to one of our allies as well as to a member of the security council of the United Nations. Then there is this statement, which is contrary to the enunciation of government policy by the Secretary of State for External Affairs last June:
The U.S., for its part, has become enmeshed in a bloody civil war in Viet Nam which cannot be justified on either moral or strategic grounds.
Sir, if ever there was a circumvention of constitutional policy that is it, because it is the antithesis of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said on June 10, 1965. I refer merely to the date; those who wish to look it up will find that the minister took the stand that this was not a civil war. Now we have a minister occupying the No. 1 position in the cabinet, the President of the Privy Council, saying this is a bloody civil war.
Then he went on to give his views with regard to bombing, burning and extermination by a foreign power which is taking place in Viet Nam. He said:
In this war, the strongest nation in the world has taken sides in a savage civil struggle and is using its tremendous power to force the other side to quit.
Such statements bring hope to communists in every part of the world, and this is an enunciation of policy by a man occupying a high and honoured position. Then he refers to
May 15, 1967	COMMONS
the fact that United States troops are obeying orders, as is their duty, and says:
Unfortunately, in a war like this, there are bound to be acts of barbarism on both sides ... If the escalation of the war continues, as seems probable, and the North Vietnamese do not give up soon, one may wonder if the United States will be driven to use nuclear bombs or to spread germs or exterminating chemicals.
If ever there was a case of urgency, this is one. If we have this discussion in the debate on the speech from the throne we can talk but we cannot get an answer from the government. Finally the minister said this:
From Canada's standpoint the grave dangers in the present situation are fourfold:
1.	The present conflict may reinforce a natural distrust of all westerners and of all white people on the part of millions of non-whites throughout the world-
2.	The second danger is that Russia and China may become reconciled as a result of their opposition to U.S. action in Viet Nam-
3.	The third danger that could result from a further escalation of the war is the direct involvement of red China-
4.	Finally, there is the gravest danger that if the United States uses nuclear weapons, the Russians would retaliate immediately.
Then he concludes:
I have read the suggestions put forward by U Thant, by our own Prime Minister, by the Honourable Paul Martin, by General Gavan, and by other thoughtful and informed Americans. They do not differ in essentials.
If ever there was a case for an instant debate, Mr. Speaker, so this government can tell us where it stands, so we may bring out from the hidden recesses the true facts of this government's policy, this is it. I say there should be an immediate debate for that reason, and because of the gross travesty on the rights of parliament when policies are enunciated outside this house which are a direct contradiction of what the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said in the last few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, though the members of this party are diametrically opposed to the terms in which the motion is couched, I think there is a case for urgency of debate with regard to the speech by the President of the Privy Council, as well as for a statement by the government with reference to Canada's position in connection with the war in Viet Nam.
The President of the Privy Council has made a statement. It is a statement we welcome, one which we think sets forth with very great clarity and realism the situation which now obtains in Southeast Asia. We feel the government should give an opportunity at the earliest possible date for a full discussion of this matter in order that the house may have an opportunity either of endorsing or repudiating the statements which have been made by the President of the Privy Council.
In his statement in Toronto he set forth the position very clearly when he said "that Canadians in all walks of life and in all political parties, including especially the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, should do all they can to press the United States to halt the bombing.'' "If we fail to do this," he said, "we must be prepared to share the responsibility of those whose policies involve the greatest risks for all mankind."
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of that clear, clarion call to all Canadians and to members of all political parties, that some opportunity ought to be given to this house to echo that call. We are not going to have an opportunity to do this, Mr. Speaker, unless the government is willing to initiate debate on the whole question. For some time we have been pressing the Prime Minister to introduce a motion in the house in order that parliament as a whole, rather than the government, may state its position on the situation in Southeast Asia. Since the government has failed to do this it seems to me that the speech made by the President of the Privy Council offers this house an excellent opportunity to have a debate and state its position. We would hope, of course, that the statement of our position would not be in the terms of

Mr. Speaker, it is unusual to set aside the order of business in this house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance. Occasionally that does happen, and obviously
May 15, 1967

there must be a serious reason for that to happen or we should continually be changing the business unexpectedly. In this instance we are justified in asking for the normal business to be set to one side to discuss a matter which has been accentuated by the speech the President of the Privy Council made on Saturday.
The speeches on the address in reply to the speech from the throne normally are diverse, covering as many subjects as are covered in the throne speech. Though international affairs and the war in Viet Nam might be dealt with during the next few days, it is significant that the government earlier refused to bring forward a resolution which would permit debate on this matter. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition on Friday urged the government to provide this opportunity for debate.
The President of the Privy Council, doing something that is most unusual for a cabinet minister, has made an enunciation of government policy without giving prior information about his intention to the House of Commons. The seriousness of this action requires that the attention of this house be focused on it. When the Secretary General of the United Nations a few days ago warned the world that there was grave probability of a third world war, many people in this country became disturbed. The President of the Privy Council has taken a stand on behalf of the government which is diametrically opposed to the policy of our closest friend and strongest ally, and jeopardizes Canada's position in international affairs and her alliance with the United States.
Those are some reasons-and there are others-for this matter which is of interest to parliament and the nation to be discussed today, that the government may clearly and decisively answer our questions on this disturbing situation.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:
I thank hon. members for their views and for the assistance they have extended to me. However, as I said at the outset after listening to the argument put forth by the Leader of the Opposition, I felt that in view of the precedents and the long established procedure accepted by all hon. members, for perhaps a hundred years, and in view of what is contained in Beauchesne it was rather obvious what decision should be reached by the Chair in the circumstances. I even hesitate to read again the well worn citation from Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 100 (3):
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate"-
This indicates that an adjournment of the ordinary business of the house is to be granted when there are no other opportunities for debate. I have no statistics to support this, and I have not looked at the precedents, but I doubt very much whether at any time in the history of the Canadian parliament the Chair has granted a motion for the adjournment of the debate on the speech from the throne for the purpose of initiating another debate. My understanding is that the debate on the speech from the throne is intended precisely to enable all hon. members to debate exactly what they wish to debate. Hon. members have all agreed that this is a matter of extreme importance and extreme urgency. In an hour or so they will all have an opportunity to debate for the rest of the morning, this afternoon and this evening the subject which has been brought to the attention of the house by the Leader of the Opposition. Representatives of all parties can do this, one after the other.
The right hon. gentleman said parliament has the right to know whether the minister was enunciating government policy, and the right to know what government policy is. He may be quite correct in this suggestion; I certainly have no right to argue with that

proposition at all. Indeed, the Leader of the Opposition has the right to ask of the Prime Minister or of someone speaking in the name of the government whether a minister speaking outside the house is enunciating the policy of the government. It is the right of any hon. member to ask such a question during the question period. But I doubt whether the granting of this motion would make it easier or more possible for the government to enunciate its policy, or whether the government would wish to do so during a debate brought about by a motion for adjournment under standing order 26 as distinct from a debate provided under the rules for consideration of the speech from the throne.
For these reasons I see no other possible determination of the matter on the part of the Chair than to refuse the motion advanced by the Leader of the Opposition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped I would be able to make a statement on orders of the day, but negotiations still are going on in Geneva. I am hopeful that later this day I will be able to ask hon. members for permission to revert to motions so I may make a full statement. However, with your tolerance, Mr. Speaker, and that of members of the house, I should like to answer this question so far as I am able to do so now.
A great measure of agreement has been reached on the main issues under discussion relative to the GATT agreements. But, as all hon. members know, it is not always the main issues which determine whether a contract can be agreed to. There still are a number of details to be worked out with respect to cereals and, until they are, one cannot be certain there will be an over-all agreement. On this point, however, I remain confident.
In the light of the fact that figures have been used so widely in the press this morning 1 think it would be well to clarify them in Canadian terms. It has been suggested that what is being agreed to in Geneva is $1.73 per bushel for No. 2 hard winter wheat at a gulf port, and that there would be a differential between No. 2 hard winter wheat and No. 1 Manitoba northern of some 22J cents a bushel. This would be a significant and welcome increase in the international minimum and maximum prices of specified qualities of wheat and would substantially strengthen arrangements for co-operation to maintain market stability for No. 1 Manitoba northern in store at the lakehead.
New maximum and minimum prices on this basis would be $1.95J and $2.38J Canadian respectively. This would represent a 21 cent increase over maximum and minimum prices

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is traditional in this debate to compliment the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am pleased to do so, not only because it is a traditional gesture but because the mover, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and the seconder, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote), delivered speeches which indicated a great deal of background research and study, and delivered them in a manner fitting the record of responsibility and sincerity they have already established in this house.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
In this debate I would like to spend the time available to me in a discussion of the dairy policy of this government, and later to make some suggestions with respect to a school milk assistance program. By and large I think the philosophy of our present dairy policy is good. Some of the details are disturbing, and I will mention them shortly in the hope that the Minister of Agriculture will have an opportunity to reflect on my suggestions.
Before making my suggestions I want to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for the generally good job he has been doing for the agricultural industry in Canada. The minister has obtained the confidence of Canadian farmers as one who is genuinely concerned with their welfare. He is concerned with the income of Canadian farmers as a whole, and he is anxious to bring it up to the standard of all Canadians. He is striving to see that all Canadians, including those in agriculture, should be able to live well, to educate their families and generally share in the good Canadian life which is being made available by this government.
Having said this I want to caution the minister on one point, and I am sure he will accept it in the spirit in which I make it. My words of caution to the minister are that he be careful about putting too much faith in the opinions of his senior officers and advisers. I
[Mr. MacEachen.l
do not say this as a criticism of the abilities or sincerity of the minister's advisers and those who hold office on various boards and commissions. However, I do suggest that these officials on some occasions may not have the practical background in agriculture which leaders of farm organizations possess. If, before announcing the new dairy policy in April, the minister and members of the Canadian Dairy Commission had given greater attention to some of the ramifications of the policy he would not now be faced with the genuine concern being experienced in the dairy industry.
Indeed, the situation we now have is that the dairy policy appears to be in conflict with the policies of other government agencies such as the Farm Credit Corporation and the ARDA administration. For example, to announce suddenly that quotas for manufacturing milk produced in 1967 and 1968 will be based on 1966-1967 production is a serious blow to those producers who have advanced plans to increase their production and move into more economically efficient units. I do not quarrel with the principle of quotas, but I do criticize strongly the practice of dealing with quotas without proper and reasonable notice being given to the producers. We are also told that quotas will be refused to producers who were not in production in 19661967. Such a drastic step without reasonable notice to the industry is surely not justifiable.
Another point of criticism I have is the lack of notice to fluid milk producers that the federal subsidy would be cut off almost overnight. I agree that the provincial governments have the essential responsibility in this field. I think, however, it would have been prudent for the federal department to have given the provinces a year in which to assume their responsibility and give notice to all, including the fluid milk producers, that the federal government would continue to pay subsidies to fluid producers in this current dairy year. The producers would then be put on notice that they had a year in which to convince the provincial governments that they should pick up the subsidies, and if the provinces indicate they would not do so the producers would then have a year in which to adjust their production as they might see fit.
In the balance of my time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal at some length with a matter which is directly related to the dairy industry but with respect to which I wish to direct a generally overriding argument, that of the health of Canadian children. I wish to
May 15. 1967

address myself not only to the Minister of Agriculture but to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The topic is that of supplying milk to Canadian school children.
I am deeply concerned over the results of official surveys made in recent years which clearly show that a large proportion of our school age children are undernourished. The strange fact is that this condition is not the result of poverty but rather seems to stem from the affluence of our society. This is borne out by D.B.S. figures which show that shipments of soft drinks between 1956 and 1966 increased by 79 per cent while fluid milk production for consumption rather than manufacturing increased by only 1.74 per cent. On a per capita basis our consumption of fluid milk has decreased in those years from 322 pounds to 264 pounds. I made a quick comparative calculation and discovered that if our per capita consumption in 1966 had remained at the 1956 level, we would have drunk 1,160 million pounds more. That is about equal to the soft drink industry's increase over that period. For every additional pound of soft drinks we consume we stop consuming an equivalent amount of nature's most perfect food, milk.
So, while the high aims toward a better life as laid out in our recent throne speech are very laudable, we need direction in how to best use our blessings. Our children need education regarding the principles of nutrition. They are eating what tastes good to them, but very often they need most what they do not like. An important step that should be taken to correct this matter is to establish now a national school milk program. This should be financed and promoted by the federal government without delay. I would like to remind the government and hon. members that this was part of the Liberal platform in 1962 and 1963, and the funds then allotted should have been augmented by now.
The need for such a program is supported by unquestionable authority. I refer you to the pamphlet "Nutrition for Health", volume III, No. 1, November 1963, published by the Ontario department of health. This describes a research program to assess the habits of adolescents carried out by the department's northwestern, Wellington and Welland units. Its results are based upon records kept of 2,436 students.
According to the minimum requirements of the ten basic food groups, as laid down by the Canada food guide-milk and cheese, eggs, meat and alternates, potatoes, vegetables,
The Address-Mr. Honey fruit, sources of vitamin C, bread, whole grain cereal and vitamin D supplements-a shocking 55 per cent, or more than 1400 students, rated "poor" to "very poor". In this group the average calculated intake of vitally needed calcium was not up to the recommended level. The report states that the neglect of milk was most serious since it is a prime source of calcium. Only 34 per cent of the boys and 25 per cent of the girls drank the amount recommended by the Canada food guide to supply adequately this food element along with the others that are supplied by milk in a near perfect combination.
The report sounded an ominous warning for girls. It stated that while growth and development may proceed normally, the bones may not be properly calcified. This brings a danger of nutritional debt which can be dangerous when pregnancy follows shortly after adolescence. The report states further that students who reported their soft drink intake averaged 3.9 bottles a week for boys and 3.4 bottles for girls. Further, the boys drank an average of 7.7 cups of coffee and tea a week while girls drank 6.9 cups.
The 1962 report of the committee for the study of the distribution of milk in the schools of the province of Quebec states that milk is an essential food for children because it is the principal source of calcium and riboflavin. It concludes that without milk a child is not adequately fed because insufficient calcium leads to many difficulties arising from poor bone formation, and can cause teeth cavities. Riboflavin is a vitamin whose need is so well documented it need not be dealt with at length here.
The findings give support to the statements made in the House of Commons on November 20, 1962. At that time I recommended, among other things, that the federal government should definitely proceed with a school milk program. I stated the government should not only support such a program financially but should sponsor education to stimulate and enthuse parents of school age children on the necessity of supplying their children with milk each day.
Today I repeat this recommendation and introduce positive suggestions as to its implementation. I am absolutely convinced it is a matter of vital importance to our nation's health and the teaching of health principles in our schools. In addition, my proposals cannot help but bring far reaching benefits to the dairy industry if they are put into effect.

May 15, 1967
The Address-Mr. Honey [DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
If we compare our distribution of school milk to that of the rest of the world we should, in this centennial year, hang our heads in shame. Here are some facts I have gathered from the publication "School Milk in Canada", published in December 1961 by the Canada Department of Agriculture. Our consumption of milk in schools accounts for less than 1 per cent of our total milk consumption, compared to 4 per cent in the United States. The Quebec report to which I referred earlier states that England, Japan, Norway, New Zealand and Sweden are equally well advanced as the United States in the areas of school milk distribution and lunches. In some of these countries the milk is provided free.
The publication "School Milk in Canada" states that the oldest successful school milk program in elementary schools in the country has been carried out by the Montreal Catholic school commission. Its efforts won national recognition in an article published by School Progress magazine entitled "Here's a Blueprint For Solving Your School's Milk Problems". That program, suggested as a model for Canada, had to be discontinued during the 1966-67 school year because the cost of milk increased and subsidy money wasn't available to make up the difference. Between one quarter and one third of the children were given milk free through benevolent efforts of service organizations and contributions by the school commission itself.
The most effective program in terms of amount of milk distributed is in Windsor, Ontario. The Department of Agriculture report states that the average consumption per pupil day in all outlets excluding vending machines, which are noted for lower turnover, is only 2 ounces per pupil day. The average of our four best cities, Montreal, Windsor, Ottawa and Hull, was less than one third of the United States figure in 1961. With the Montreal Catholic schools discontinuing their program, at least temporarily, the situation has become worse.
United States consumption averages 5.8 ounces per pupil day, the Canada Department of Agriculture report states. It also affirms that if United States methods were used here we could probably raise Canada's over-all consumption to a desirable 5 ounces per pupil day.
There is little doubt that our low consumption results to a large extent from the high prices our children must pay. Spectacular results occur when prices are lowered. The

Department of Agriculture report tells about studies made in St. Louis, and in the state of Wisconsin. In St. Louis when federal subsidy permitted the price for an 8 ounce container to be lowered from 7J cents to 3 cents, consumption increased 180 per cent. In Wisconsin when elementary school prices were dropped from 6 cents to 3 cents per 8 ounces, sales increased by 208 per cent.
The number of children participating in Wisconsin was 100 per cent when the price ranged from 0 to 0.9 cents per carton. At 3 cents to 3.9 cents it was 79.3 per cent. Canada's school milk participation by students, averaging about 20 per cent, looks very sick by comparison. Despite all pressures of its international commitments the United States is not disturbing this activity. Last year, according to an article in the Economist magazine, President Johnson asked for $20 million for school milk and Congress raised the amount to $100 million.
Mr. Ronald H. Clark, proprietor of Clark Dairy Limited of Ottawa, stated in a speech to the National Dairy Council meeting on March 21 of this year that he doubts that a single dairy in Canada, trading solely in fresh milk and cream, is earning a profit. Profits, such as they are, come from other products. The average earnings on sales by the dairy industry is 1.9 per cent compared to 4.9 per cent in all manufacturing industries, Mr. Clark said. The low profit position of this industry makes it impossible for it to assist school milk programs by lowering prices. Such action was suggested by the Quebec provincial committee studying school milk distribution in its 1962 report, and no doubt others have made similar proposals that arise from the assumption that there are significant profits to be reduced.
Another suggestion made by this committee was that low cost school milk would stimulate the lagging desire by the children for it, and that dairies should look upon the cost of their assistance through lower prices as part of sales promotion and advertising costs. The sad state of the industry rules out this suggestion also. Mr. T. B. Cooper, president of the National Dairy Council, stated this year that sales charts for the past 10 years show a lack of promotion spending on products using the most milk. He explained that the profit situation did not allow such activity, while the promotion budgets for alternates and substitutes show an ever increasing trend.
Promoting the drinking of milk by children is an activity that will bring the ultimate in
May 15, 1967

The Address-Mr. Mandziuk war. During the period from 1956 to 1961, for instance, the number of dairy farmers dropped from 398,604 to 308,980.
We are proud of Canada, Mr. Speaker, as a great and modem country where our people generally are well paid and our families enjoy a high standard of living. Many of us have assumed that because of this our children are well fed and do not need milk in school. The facts prove that they not only need milk but require education as to why they should drink it.
Our dairy industry is suffering because of a declining per capita consumption of milk. A school milk assistance bill will provide the most effective means to reverse this trend. It will bring back a desire for milk in today's children. It will give these children knowledge about the vital role played by milk in their own good health. Then they in turn will see to it that their children, the next generation, will not return to the bad habits of today.
This is a matter of great national importance, Mr. Speaker. I suggest it should be the prime concern of the Department of National Health and Welfare as well as departments of health in the various provinces.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I make the plea that we catch up with the other advanced nations of the world in the area of school milk distribution. Our reason should be the same as Australia's when it established its states grants act in 1950 to provide milk to school children. It gave its reasons as "to help maintain their health and establish milk as part of their daily diet".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with may I express our admiration and appreciation of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and those who piloted us through the marathon session that has just ended. We regret that this house has not been able to give them a well deserved holiday. I also wish to congratulate the mover of the address, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson), and to state that the contents of his remarks and the manner of their delivery could well be the envy of many of the front benchers in this house.
I also wish to congratulate the seconder of the address on his speech. His eloquence was very appealing, but he launched into a criticism of Conservative agricultural policy and sang the praises of the policy of the present Liberal government. I suggest he read the address just delivered so ably by the hon. member who preceded me, the hon. member

for Durham (Mr. Honey). His eyes might be opened to the failure of the present government to carry out its election promises. I also suggest to the seconder that he must have failed to read the record of the Conservative administration from 1957 to 1962, because he would have learnt that the idea of Expo, about which Canada is so enthusiastic today, as well as its present location, originated with the administration headed by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I would further point out that the Saskatchewan river dam would never have been conceived, let alone built, had the Liberals continued in the drivers' seat, as they are today; and they are now very happy to see this project being completed. They are also very happy to name it after a Liberal. They did not have the courtesy to name it after the man who really initiated the dam, a project which the Liberals were afraid to touch. It must also not be forgotten that crop insurance, cash advances to farmers, ARDA and other measures originated with the Conservative government, measures which this government have tried but failed to improve. I think credit should be given where credit is due.
With regard to Canada's one hundredth anniversary, it is marvellous to see how enthusiastically those who were born in Canada as well as those who have entered the country more recently have joined together in the celebration of our centennial. And well they might, because few who were born in 1867 are still living to celebrate our hundredth birthday. I also suggest that few who were born either this year or last year will live to celebrate our second hundredth anniversary. They must therefore make the most of this occasion, and I am glad all have taken our celebrations to heart.
I realize that on occasions such as this we must pause to take stock, to make a short resume of the past in order to understand the present. We think we have difficulties and face problems, but I feel we should understand how these problems arose in order to get some inkling of how perhaps we can best find solutions. The history of Canada did not begin just one hundred years ago, Mr. Speaker. If my memory serves me correctly the history of Canada began 475 years ago. It started with the landing of Jacques Cartier and the hardy French explorers and pioneers who broke the first sod and lived through indescribable hardships in the early days of this country. They were the ones who laid the foundations for this nation. We cannot forget
May 15, 1967

or ignore these people because, as I say, Canada was not born just 100 years ago.
To these people, Mr. Speaker, I take off my hat. I cannot help but point out that it was these same French pioneers who firmly implanted in this land their language, their culture and their religion, which still exist to this day. They should be very proud of the fact that their cultural heritage which they brought from their motherland of France is still adhered to to this day.
The British conquest in 1763 made very few changes to New France; the only change was in the name. After the British conquest British servicemen stayed in the country, and after the American revolution many United Empire Loyalists settled in what was then Upper Canada, now Ontario. The Germans, Dutch and Swiss came after the British, and in 1799 German speaking Mennonites came to Ontario. They show that they are still among the best farmers in Canada. One year earlier, in 1798, the Irish came.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Anybody who maintains that at confederation, in 1867, only English and French were here is twisting history and not telling the truth, because there were at least seven ethnic groups in Canada at that time. Apart from the English there were Irish, Scottish, German, Dutch, Swiss and others. Whether they were consulted about confederation is something else.
Shortly before confederation we saw a Selkirk settlement in Manitoba, and in 1877, ten years after confederation, the German Mennonites came to Manitoba. They have proved themselves the best of farmers. All these people made a considerable imprint on Canadian life, entering the civil service, politics, the judiciary and the teaching profession. They have been a credit to this country. The same can be said of the first Icelandic immigrants who came to Manitoba in 1875, five years before it was organized into a province. It is not difficult to find descendants of these people occupying high posts in the civil service and provincial and federal governments.
Seventy five years ago last year the Ukrainians came, and last year they celebrated that seventy fifth anniversary. Politicians and outstanding persons of Ukrainian origin took part in the celebrations lauding the achievements of the group which is now half a million strong. Seventy six years ago, with no physical resources, the Ukrainians came as poor immigrants from the Austro-Hungarian and Russian part of the Ukraine

The Address-Mr. Mandziuk because they were oppressed economically and politically. They were men in sheepskin coats who were ridiculed and laughed at; their women wore babushkas. Today what lady in Canada is shy about wearing such head covering?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They set the fashion.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I bow my head to the pioneer Ukrainian women who helped their husbands to build homesteads in parts of the country without roads, who lived in small shacks and brought up children while their husbands went away to earn money with which to buy farm implements. Those women helped to clear the land. Those people have survived. Have they contributed nothing to this nation? I can easily prove my point. We see descendants of Ukrainian origin in every facet of Canadian life, and they enjoy the privileges and rights of citizenship which their forefathers undertook to uphold when they became settlers.
Old loyalties had not worn off when the first world war came. It was too soon after the immigration; yet records show that 10,000 of Ukrainian origin joined the Canadian forces in answer to the call. One man who had worked in the House of Commons before his death several years ago was of Ukrainian origin and won the Victoria Cross. His name was Konowal. In the second world war 40,000 sons and grandsons of the first pioneers from the Ukraine answered the call and served in Canada's forces. Some reached high rank; some were decorated; all have been a credit.
In saying these words I pay the same compliment to the peoples of all ethnic groups in Canada. After one generation the sons and daughters of every ethnic group become Canadians. They know no other land, and having made this land their home they hope to make it better for the future.
I am about to quote from the Prime Minister. May I call it one o'clock?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wish to quote from a speech which the Prime Minister delivered in
May 15, 1967

The Address-Mr. Mandziuk
Edmonton on July 17, 1966 on the occasion of the 75 th anniversary of Ukrainian immigration to Canada. In the presence of some 25,000 people he said:
You have continued the faith of your forefathers. Through the years you have maintained your own identity, your culture and your institutions, inside the Canadian nation. You have enriched Canada greatly by your contributions to its political, cultural, agricultural, industrial, professional, educational development. Your love of the land; your passion for freedom, personal and national; your belief in democracy-these have been captured and expressed in your poetry, your songs and dances. These are now part of Canada's heritage.
By preserving your own identity, therefore, your own language and traditions, you have added something of value, of strength and colour, to the Canadian character.
These words could be addressed to any of the ethnic groups which have found their home in Canada. They would apply to Canadians of Italian origin. They would apply to the Poles and all the others; I do not restrict myself to any particular group. The wonderful part of it is that all these various ethnic groups have adopted a common language so they can understand each other. In most cases, they have adopted the English language. They have established trust and confidence in each other; they have exchanged cultural habits; they have intermarried. All are playing their part in the development of this nation.
On behalf of all those of ethnic origin, people who compose around 26 per cent of the Canadian population, I take issue with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who concluded a statement he made on March 4 by saying that Canada will never be one people with one dream. We who are of ethnic origin believe Canada is becoming a country of one people with one dream, if it has not yet become so.
I agree with the attitude taken by a great Canadian, Hon. J. T. Thorson, Chancellor of the Exchequer Court and at one time a minister in the federal government. In an article which appeared in the Edmonton Journal, we read the following:
The Honourable J. T. Thorson, former chief justice of the Exchequer Court, said in Edmonton this week that Canada is being "brainwashed" into believing it is a bilingual country. It is not, it never has been and, as Mr. Justice Thorson said, bilingualism as a national policy is not in the national interest.
Hon. members may wish to know what is my own attitude toward bilingualism. I believe in it, my understanding of the phrase being that it means knowing two languages. Ethnic groups in Canada have adopted this

point of view. Bearing in mind the words spoken by the Prime Minister to that Ukrainian gathering in Edmonton, every ethnic group has the right or possibly the obligation to maintain its language and propagate its culture as well as to learn one of the official languages, either English or French. Maybe it will not suit some people but most of the ethnic groups in Canada have adopted the English language. Some of them, a good 25 per cent, use the English language to the extent that it has even become the mother tongue in the home.
What will Canada be like 100 years from now? I am sure the fathers of confederation, when they were trying to mould this country into a united dominion, could not have foreseen what conditions would be like 100 years in the future. They could not have foreseen that Canada would develop from a colony of Britain into a completely sovereign and independent state. We cannot be sure what Canada will be like a hundred years from now when the second anniversary of confederation comes around. Who can foretell?
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Of course there are forecasts. There are those who doubt whether there will be a Canada at all. Some feel that Canada will be absorbed by the United States. Some feel that we are now dependent upon the United States economically and therefore will become a part of that great nation. Some believe we should have a two nation structure. They envisage something like the situation which existed m respect of Austria and Hungary up to the end of the first world war. I and most Canadians believe-and it is safe for us to prognosticate because we will not live to celebrate another hundredth anniversary and will not be called to account-that Canada geographically will remain what it is today. I believe it will be completely independent, despite rumblings to the contrary. It will be a powerful nation of one hundred million people at least, fearing no one. Those who live to celebrate the two hundredth anniversary will feel proud of this nation. Canada will have one way of life. We now are laying the foundations for a distinctive Canadian culture containing the best of all cultures. We have contributions from those from other nations who have been here and have developed their own cultures.
Today we damn, condemn and fight among ourselves; we do almost anything to try to put Canada in a strait-jacket. Some people say Canada never will be anything but what it is
May 15, 19G7

now. Other people say that Canada is a nation already or, if it is not, that it is in the process of becoming one. As I have said, a two nation concept would be logical were it not for two historical facts. History cannot be denied. When this nation entered confederation there were seven ethnic groups. In addition, because of the open door policy of this nation, millions and millions of other people have come to this country. We must treat this nation as a whole containing many varieties of races, many varieties of cultures, and people with many varieties of ideas. The newcomers to this nation who brought with them their cultural heritage assumed their full obligations as Canadian citizens. In return for assuming those obligations as Canadian citizens they have a right to expect, and were given that right, the same rights and privileges enjoyed by those who came before and those who had been here for generations.
In peace and war these people have not at all been lagging behind the others who claim a special status because their forefathers had been in this nation for generations. These newcomers have integrated into the new life. They have shown that they can perform their essential duties. All they ask in return is that their opinions be heard, that they have a hand in shaping Canada and in determining what it will be during the next one hundred years. Otherwise they will be second class citizens who, in spite of the obligations they have assumed, will have no rights.
The trend followed by this government is to ignore these other people. I will not mention a name, but one politician when speaking to a Jewish ethnic group a year and a half ago said-and I will paraphrase-that all the other peoples in Canada must accept the language and culture of either the English or French groups or else. He did not finish the "or else". Where does that put us? I do not like referring to the third force; it is not that. These other groups of Canadians have the same rights as those who had been here for hundreds of years. They are here because they were invited and welcomed.
Mind you, all these groups who came here did not have their passage subsidized. They suffered the hardships of pioneer life; they have done much more, and have assumed all their duties in this nation. They must have all their rights. Whatever Canada is to become in the future, they feel they should have a voice. As I have said already, this government does not consider them full fledged citizens. Rather they are considered to be second class citizens.
The Address-Mr. Mandziuk
History repeats itself. Other nations have gone through the same process. They have developed from a mixture of various cultures. We might take the example of Great Britain, which went through these throes and finally became one nation. This is what we are in the process of doing in Canada. It is difficult to tell what Canada will be like in one hundred years from now, but as I said I have every hope. During centennial year I think we should instil in our minds the fact that we are going to work for a strong, united Canada.
There are two other matters I should like to mention. They are unrelated but may affect Canadians as a whole. This year on October 5 the Soviet union will be celebrating the anniversary of its revolution. Here in Canada we have many people who came from behind the iron curtain. These people will be celebrating the fiftieth anniversary of liberation. They had gained freedom but lost it because of the iron curtain. I know many persons, and this includes ministers of the crown, who will be asked or who have been asked to speak at these various functions. We should keep in mind that these persons should not be accused of having a double allegiance or anything like that. They cannot help but have strong feelings about the fate of the land of their fathers or forefathers. Canadians express concern about what happens in the Congo and what happens in Viet Nam today. Why should these people, whether they be Russian, Ukrainian, Polish, Czechoslovakian, or whatever their origin, not be understood in the same way? Why should this sympathetic feeling not be expressed in respect of these people and what is happening behind the iron curtain?
Another thing which disturbs me as a Canadian is that in this country we have certain groups which lead protest marches against the United States for what goes on in Viet Nam. Show me one group in Canada which leads these protest marches against the United States in Viet Nam which at the same time leads protest marches against the U.S.S.R. which is supplying armaments to North Viet Nam, and against China which is also supplying armaments to North Viet Nam. Why should there be no protest against them? I cannot understand why Canadians are so gullible. Perhaps these protest marches are communist inspired; I do not know.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I cannot understand why the United States is damned and condemned just because it is
May 15, 1967

The Address-Mr. Badanai the bulwark of the free world against communist aggression. Had it not been for what the United States has done in NATO we would not today have a free western Europe. Today the United States is preventing the further spread of communism in Southeast Asia. Some people get carried away in their protests against the United States, but I suggest in all fairness they should protest against the U.S.S.E. Where are the Migs made which are fighting against United States boys if they are not made in the U.S.S.R.?
