maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the people of the constituencies of Bu-rin-Burgeo and Nicolet-Yamaska for electing two outstanding representatives to the House of Commons. They can feel proud of their members' performances in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I have never heard better presentations delivered in this house during the nine years I have been a member. I heartily congratulate them.
The tradition of moving the address in reply was greatly enhanced by the remarkable message of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, which could not have been more appropriate for the beginning of this centennial session. It has provided a splendid opportunity to dwell on some of the aspects of the history of this glorious land. The right hon. leader of the official opposition and the Prime Minister dealt with the subject with an eloquence which I do not presume to approach. They dealt with the years of Sir John A. Macdonald, and the hon. member who just spoke dealt with the history of some of the ethnic groups which have immigrated to Canada. With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I intend to go further back to the days when the white man met the red man on the coast of Newfoundland and the shores of Quebec.
Being one of the few members of this house who came to Canada as an immigrant I find this an occasion which inspires me to say that Canadians of other than Anglo-Saxon and

French origin have a special feeling for Canada. I need not remind anyone in this house that five years after the discovery of America by Christopher Columbus another Italian mariner, Giovanni Cabot, in the service of King Henry VII of England and in honour of his native city of Venice, planted the Venetian banner of St. Mark side by side with the British flag on Canadian soil. It is interesting to know that the exploit brought him fame but no fortune. King Henry, grateful but stingy, paid John Cabot ten pounds sterling, the equivalent at the present rate of exchange of approximately $30, for the discovery of Canada.
Although Britain and France are recognized as the two founding nations, neither country can claim credit for the first person to set foot on our shores. Some people claim that the Norsmen were the first Europeans to set foot on our soil 500 years before the flag of Britain was planted in Canada. If this is true they left no records and told nobody about it. The fact remains that the British flag was planted in Canada not by an Englishman but by an Italian. And without taking away any glory from Jacques Cartier, who is generally recognized as the first man to explore New France, it was another Italian, Giovanni de Ver-razano, who led an expedition to Cape Breton in 1524.
But if Britain and France were not the first to arrive here, they were the two nations which did most to build our country and give us our laws and customs, and for this reason they alone are considered Canada's founding races.
The next Italians to come to Canada were mainly soldiers, priests and artists. There was Enrico Tonti known as Henry DeTonti, whose father Lorenzo, a Neopolitan living in France, invented the tontine, a complex pension scheme or annuity. Henry DeTonti, who had lost one hand in battle and wore an iron substitute, earning him the nickname "Main Defer", was LaSalle's faithful lieutenant and played a large part in the great French explorer's success.
When Montreal's existence was threatened by the Iroquois Indians in 1665, France sent out the famous Carignan-Salieres regiment. Part of that thousand man unit was raised in Savoia, and most of the soldiers and officers were Italians. The regiment was ordered back to Europe three years later, but 400 members remained in New France as settlers. Taking courage from the departure of the soldiers, the Iroquois Indians renewed their attempts
May 15. 1967

The Address-Mr. Badanai
to destroy Montreal. They wiped out the settlements of Lachine and La Chesnaye and stood posed for massacre in Montreal in 1691, when they were roundly defeated by a militia force one of whose leaders was the Italian Captain Tommasco Crisafe.
The most illustrious Italian in New France, which as everyone knows is now Quebec, was Francesco Burlamacchi, knows as Francois de Bourlamaque, third in command after Montcalm, the famous French general who died on the Quebec heights in the battle fought on the Plains of Abraham and Levis. He was in charge at Montreal after the defeat of Montcalm and surrendered to the English only on the orders of General Vaudreuil. He returned to France, where he agitated long but with no success for a reconquest of Canada, and ended his days as governor of the island of Guadeloupe. The mining town of Bourlamaque, Quebec is named in his honour.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
As everyone knows, one of the stipulations of confederation which brought Upper Canada and British Columbia together was the building of a railway system from coast to coast. This condition of federation brought large numbers of immigrants to Canada from Italy, Germany, the Ukraine, Poland and many other countries of Europe to build the C.P.R., the Great Northern and the Grand Trunk, the latter two forming the present Canadian National Railways. To accomplish this tremendous undertaking, when machines were unknown and everything had to be done by hand, pick and shovel, much cheap labour was needed. Italian labour agencies were set up and workers hired by the shipload. By 1900 there were in Canada 11,000 families of Italian origin.
Immigrants from many lands, the forerunners of hundreds of thousands who were to follow during the course of this century, sailed up the St. Lawrence to the promised land of Canada. They came with great expectations which for only a few were ever fulfilled, but by their toil and sweat they laid the rails to form the link that was to unite Canada. They were mostly single men, or men who had left their families behind hoping to become rich, but few returned and many never saw their families again.
At the time of confederation, 100 years ago, Canada had a population of little more than three million, and of these only 8 per cent were of origins other than English and French. In our last national census of 1961 the British ratio had shrunk to 43.8 per cent, 27053-14
the French was 34.4 per cent, while people of other nationalities represented 25 per cent. These facts should remind us that Canada, in the words of our Prime Minister "is not a country of two races only, of two cultures and traditions, but a country of many races and many cultures and many traditions. We are fortunate in our multiple heritage, in the challenge that comes from building a united country, one with the strength and richness that comes from diversity."
The 25 per cent of non-British and nonFrench origin may well become the cement binding the founding races into a composite whole, and achieve that unity of purpose which the Fathers of Confederation hoped to achieve. Senator Paul Yuzyk in his book "Ukrainian Canadians", which I think was published only recently, in a chapter entitled "Partnership of the Canadian Elements" has this to say:
Canada was conceived as a country of plural culture. Her self government and independence were gradually achieved by the co-operation of the French and British peoples through our parliamentary institutions and common allegiance to the crown, which has been the binding force throughout the history of Canada.
Our common experience of the land, the history, the democratic institutions and the economic prosperity has developed a spirit of pride and unity in Canada, which is equally shared by Canadians of all origins, who have also made contributions to Canada's progress. As the concept of equality evolved, the British and French in free association emerged as partners. The idea of partnership is gradually being extended to the other ethnic groups, which can only serve to enhance Canadian unity, rather than weaken it as is believed by some sceptics and pessimists.
The beginning of the second century is a good time to consider a resurgence in the development of cur country. The development of a ribbon of civilization above the 49th parallel received the attention of our Canadian pioneers in the first century of our history, and as this widened further north, unlocking vast treasures of timber and minerals, and settlements prospered on the prairies, it was a period of great achievement which the generous immigration policy at the beginning of the century made possible. I venture to say that if successive governments had kept an open door immigration policy after the first great war we would today have a population not of 20 million but of 40 million. Only recently, since this government took office, has there been a more realistic immigration policy which has made it possible to almost triple the number of immigrants admitted to Canada in 1966 from a low of 72,000 in 1962.
May 15, 1967

The Address-Mr. Badanai
I have been rather critical of the immigration policy of the former Conservative government for lack of vision concerning immigration. I have consistently advocated a more generous policy to encourage people to make their home in Canada. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration is to be congratulated for accepting several recommendations of the joint Senate and House of Commons committee on immigration designed to allow prospective immigrants to enter Canada without the skills and educational standards contained in the white paper, with a modification of sponsorship regulations which were considered too drastic if applied according to the original draft of the white paper. Canada needs men and women with skills, but equally the need for unskilled persons, if not as great today as at the beginning of the century is nevertheless substantial and important to the development of our country.
Indeed, Canada's history is laced with the story of people from many lands coming to Canada in search of peace, freedom and prosperity, building a new life; people from every country of the globe and from every walk of life enriching Canada with character and tradition. I anticipate that with the approval of legislation based on the committee's recommendations the annual number of immigrants will be no less than 1 per cent of the total population, which will ensure the admittance of at least 200,000 per year. I maintain that is a modest figure but is relatively substantial and, all things considered is a great improvement over the early years of the 1960's.
The opposition characterized the throne speech as a rehash, which can be interpreted as the ranting of frustrated politicians. Unbiased people will look at it objectively and see in it many good measures designed to give Canadians good, sound government.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The promised revision of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, as an example, is a heart warming decision. The act dates back to 1908 and has remained virtually unchanged since 1929. It is badly out of date and unduly harsh on young people. The changes will include authority to juvenile courts to make fuller use of probation and parole services and suspended sentences.
The John Howard and Elizabeth Fry societies are doing a tremendous job with most limited and inadequate financial resources, and here I wish to appeal to the government to be less stingy in granting financial assistance to these societies, which are composed of

Holland, which parole 80 per cent of their inmates, 52 per cent of whom complete their parole satisfactorily while in Canada less than 15 per cent are paroled, and of this small number half are paroled to the John Howard agency with 10 per cent of that number completing parole successfully. Our penal institutions are crowded, our jails are overflowing, and we must spend millions of dollars to build better and bigger jail houses.
The John Howard society, with its fine record of rehabilitation, could do much to eliminate this overpopulation in jails if it were given reasonable grants from this government. The Thunder Bay society with its extremely limited budget handles six parolees a year and less than 100 annually of those who complete their sentences. Their success rate is high, but without guidance from the Ontario society and a professional case worker they cannot begin to perform the required job. Should the government move toward mandatory parole, which is being studied now by the attorney general, how could an agency such as this one even begin to do an adequate job? The board of directors of this society is very concerned and hopes the government will consider most seriously a generous grant to the John Howard and Elizabeth Fry societies which serve the whole district of Thunder Bay, including the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur, the record of which in providing parolees with direction, shelter, clothing and jobs is second to none in Canada.
Such hon. members have been complaining about the length of the speech from the throne. May I suggest to you, sir, that in the nine years I have had the privilege of sitting in this chamber I have never heard a throne speech with so many references to consequential legislation designed to assist the economy of the nation in every sphere of national activity as the one delivered by the new Governor General.
In the development of incentive programs I urge the government to extend the designated area to include northwestern Ontario, a 200,000 square mile area of great natural resources, many of which are still untapped. Northwestern Ontario has been more or less neglected in favour of the more affluent eastern parts of the province. I suggest to the Minister of Defence Production that he give consideration to the resolution of the Northwestern Ontario Municipal Association, the Northwestern Ontario Associated Chambers of Commerce and the Northwestern Ontario Development Council urging the 27053-141
The Address-Mr. Ormiston establishment of incentives to industry because, in the light of the obvious fact that industry is going where the free gifts are, these three groups have had more to do with the development of northwestern Ontario than any others. They state that none of the measures taken so far have proved effective and that this resource-filled area is being bypassed and ignored even though it qualifies as a development area in every apparent way.
Not only is the designated area program denied to northwestern Ontario but every suggestion toward an area-based handling of such aids to industry is turned down. The northwestern Ontario area desires an incentive program to attract secondary industry, business and individuals.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The proposal to amend the Indian Act to benefit the Indian and Eskimo people should be welcomed by every member of this house. Being a member of the standing committee on Indian affairs I have a particular interest in the welfare of our original Canadians. Of course I am not alone in appreciating the government's concern in accelerating assistance in an effort to secure for them greater participation in the affairs of the nation.
The legislation to provide long term loans to agricultural and fisheries associations to permit them to develop facilities is indeed a welcome move. This government has done a great deal for agriculture since it took power, and the announcement of the establishment of a special task force under the Minister of Agriculture and the broadening of the Farm Credit Act are also measures that the farmers of my constituency, and no doubt many other constituencies, will appreciate and welcome.
The promotion of consumer interests will include the designation of a department of corporate and consumer affairs. This feature will have the effect of stabilizing consumer prices and prevent the spiralling cost of commodities affecting every household in the country. These are only a few of the 30-odd items contained in the speech from the throne for the specific purpose of making life for the Canadian people easier and happier. In the words of the Prime Minister I say:
-the speech from the throne reflects in general terms the need for government to improve the opportunities for every Canadian to live a better life.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, may I be permitted to particularly
May 15, 1967

The Address-Mr. Ormiston
commend the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) upon his masterful maiden speech. His effort was outstanding and appeared even more remarkable when compared with the document he was interpreting. I suppose it is only normal for government members to find much more cause for enthusiasm in the speech from the throne than members of the opposition. We on this side, without too much trouble, can recall other speeches from the throne and other legislative programs which produced more disillusionment than ecstacy.
The pith of the throne speech, if it can be called such, in this centennial year was a preamble on our hundred years' history which sounded more like a conducted tour of a factory than the description of the emergence of a nation. The lavish description of our contemporary social, cultural and economic environment is exceeded only by the dynamic and challenging future which will come about as a result of the implementation of the added superlatives, pious platitudes and worn out cliches which together are the framework of this current document. This speech, like the authors, is trying to provide all things to all people, and in its desperate attempt to cover every field of endeavour the government is becoming more socialist than the socialists. In so doing the government is crowding the private enterprise sector of our economy into ever narrowing and restrictive limits.
This country of ours was built largely by the efforts of free and private enterprise, and it is sad and humiliating for a Conservative to be present and watch a government which finds hanging so obnoxious but permits the slow strangulation of our traditional economic system and the erosion of our hereditary symbols. There is nothing in the speech from the throne which provides any positive proof that closer ties with the commonwealth are advantageous, that the monarchy provides the best type of parliamentary government or that our constitution which has stood the test of time could not be improved by judicious amendment.
A nation needs a strong spirit as well as a healthy body, but if the body politic is partisan and amoral, the body social dependent and sterile, no amount of legislative action can heal and no amount of penance absolve. A young country in order to expand and develop needs strong initiative from its people, but this will not be developed by the introduction of a guaranteed annual income

or any scheme to give cradle to the grave protection supplied by a paternal government.
My leader, in the course of his timely and enlightened contribution, pointed out some of the omissions in the speech from the throne, but his chivalrous treatment of this document indicated that without continuing support from its sponsors it might well collapse from the weight of its own preponderance. It has been noted that while there have been no rave notices in the newspapers on the content of the speech, neither have there been any wholesale condemnations. There has, however, from all quarters been indifferent and desultory sniping indicative of an elusive and indefinite target.
The most tangible contents seem to have originated in committees by way of recommendations during the past year, or in private members' bills which emanated from the backbenches, so long overlooked. One would have thought, too, that in centennial year those who made a contribution to the peace and safety of our country might well have been given some consideration. The veterans, however, seem to have been forgotten. On more than one occasion members of this party have put forward some sound ideas for the improvement of the Pension Act. While it may be conducive to orderly planning to wait for the report of the Wood commission before making any changes, it should be borne in mind that contrary to the words of the old wartime song, old soldiers do not live forever.
The treatment of the veteran is not unique; while the government transports us in flights of fancy, in esthetic dreams of cultural ecstasy, the material things of life which sustain the average individual are daily becoming more costly to obtain. The ever increasing rise in the cost of living, coupled with a similar rise in the cost of production, is nowhere more visible than in the agricultural industry. The proposed march on Ottawa by eastern farmers must be looked upon with sympathy by Canadian farmers in general because the agricultural sector is one area of our economy where the cost of production has far outstripped returns to the producer.
The fact that the government has proposed a special task force for agriculture indicates that some concern is held for the future of this industry. However, some guide lines are needed if those who may form this combat group of Joe Greene's giants can be expected to produce anything constructive. While the special task force can do little to influence the
May 15, 1967

Kenndy round of trade negotiations where the cereals committee of GATT is concerned, or to initiate any action under the I.W.A., there are definite fields in which improvement can take place. For instance, the beef industry will soon be in jeopardy unless thousands of acres of pasture land are found in the immediate future. This country will be importing beef in three years unless suitable grazing land is found to support the cattle which will be needed to meet our increasing demands.
The transportation and storage facilities for agricultural products might also be examined. There has been little change in our livestock and grain cars in the last 60 years. Our country elevators are certainly not models of efficiency, and it does not seem unreasonable to expect that one or two modern elevators at each shipping point would be much more effective than the number that are in operation to meet present day requirements. It also seems absurd that thousands of bushels of dockage is shipped to the terminal elevators every year, thus wasting time, space and money when this by-product could be utilized in local feed lots and by local industry in the form of prepared stock feeds. If at any time this anticipated force is in any doubt as to the path of progress, it might well investigate those responsible for the construction of dams in Saskatchewan and why they were not named accordingly.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
However, a serious situation has developed in Saskatchewan and it is this. At present P.F.R.A. officials are unable to proceed with needed projects because of the inability of the government to decide which department is responsible for the very essential programs which in the past have been the responsibility of the Department of Agriculture but are now disseminated among the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Forestry and the Department of Agriculture. The Prime Minister has said this is an important question, and since adequate supplies of fresh water are one of our greatest assets it behooves the government to make the necessary decisions as soon as possible in order that these water and land conservation projects may be proceeded with at the earliest convenience. With the conclusions of work on the South Saskatchewan river dam the P.F.R.A. authorities will be available for other extensive works, and they should not be kept in ignorance because of indecision on the part of government departments.
The Address-Mr. Brewin
Our agricultural industry and its potential is in the hands of Canadian citizens, and the same could be said of our other industries if Canadians had confidence in their own future. Canadians are the world's greatest savers. By investing in our own future, by expanding our industries, by extending our trade to all parts of the world, by processing our materials at home and by the proper inducements to save for ownership, we will not only own the corporations that develop our wealth but will be supplying capital to others as well. The benefits of corporate capitalism have been well demonstrated. They have raised not only the level of our own living standards but forced socialistic countries to re-examine their economic systems as well.
The occasion of our Canadian centennial invites us to examine the progress of the last hundred years. But it also invites us to remember that Abraham Lincoln was assassinated a little over a hundred years ago. Legend has it that he once spoke these wise and eloquent words:
You cannot bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift. You cannot help the wage earner by pulling down the wage payer. You cannot build character and courage by taking away man's initiative and independence. You cannot help men permanently by doing for them what they could and should do for themselves.
This is a philosophy which can be accepted by all men of good faith no matter of what political affiliation, and if applied in this centennial year as a basis of progress for the future the higher standards of quality and service, honour and integrity, will be well served by this and succeeding parliaments.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join the other members who have preceded me in this debate in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address on their excellent speeches. Before turning to the main subject matter of my remarks I should like to congratulate the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) on what he recently said about the war in Viet Nam. I should like to re-echo his words when he said "I believe all of us have a duty to record our growing horror over what is going on in Viet Nam. If the present policy leads to disaster, the extermination of millions of unfortunate Vietnamese, or possibly global nuclear war, our failure to speak out will always remain on our conscience."
I find it hard to phrase a more scathing indictment of the government of which the President of the Privy Council remains a member. Their policy in this issue has been
May 15, 1967

The Address-Mr. Brewin one of mute, inglorious neutrality, of silence in the face of some of the greatest moral issues which have faced this or any other generation.
The recurring theme in this debate has been future constitutional arrangements for Canada, and this is the matter I should like to discuss. The celebration of 100 years of our history as a nation provides the occasion for a look at our fundamental institutions, a look backward that can be one of gratitude and thankfulness for our growth as a nation, and a look forward that enables us to assess whether we need changes for the future.
The constitution, as all hon. members know, is the fundamental law or framework within which our governments operate. The powers conferred on governments by the constitution and the limitations imposed on governments by the constitution are of the utmost practical importance to all Canadians. In my view there is a need for change in our constitution, not necessarily radical change but nevertheless change that is real.
In our view, Mr. Speaker, our confederation will be seriously endangered if we are not prepared to make the necessary changes but accept the static and laissez faire attitude which seems to dominate the thinking at the present government. Constitutions, of course, by reason of the fact that they represent the fundamental law of the country, cannot be subjected to constant change; they do require a degree of permanency. But they are human institutions, and as such should not be considered immutable or unamendable. As we all know, our present constitution is the British North America Act, a statute passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom as long ago as 1867, a time when Canada consisted of a group of isolated colonies with agricultural economies totally different from the modern industrialized society that is Canada today.
As all members of the house realize, the British North America Act has been amended in small details from time to time and then, of course, has followed the due process of interpretation by the courts. But there are two reasons, in our view, for changing our constitution. The first is that it is an obsolete document. This is not surprising. Indeed, it would be strange if a document which was drafted to fit the circumstances of a group of isolated agricultural colonies a century ago remained appropriate in the totally different context of a modern industrial nation. It is trite to point out that we are living in a world of constant and rapid world-wide change. The functions

of government today are totally different from the functions of government 100 years ago.
The second basic reason, in our view, that we need a new look at our constitution arises out of the crisis-an overworked word, perhaps-caused by the emergence of what has been called the quiet revolution in Quebec. It does not seem to me a particularly appropriate phrase because it has not been particularly quiet, and I do not think "revolution" is a very apt word. But the fact is clear-and I think this should be welcomed by all Canadians-that a new spirit, a new and vigorous sense of identity, is abroad in the province of Quebec and among French speaking Canadians generally.
Some people seem to think that the sense of discontent in Quebec will just go away if we do not bother about it. Indeed, that seems to be the attitude of the present government.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I prefer the view expressed by men such as Claude Ryan of Le Devoir, by the 15 members of the B and B commission, by the premier of Quebec and by many others when they tell us that the aspirations of Quebec have created a genuine crisis and for a solution require revisions to our constitution. Mr. Ryan, editor of Le Devoir, a few weeks ago said that Quebec was not eager to secede from Canada but desired expression in the constitution of a clearer and more satisfactory status. In his view the articles of the constitution need to be gone over one by one and a definition drawn of the new status. I am convinced that we ignore the pleas of such well informed and devoted Canadians as Mr. Ryan at out peril.
What are some of the fundamentals of our constitutional structure that we should take account of in the process of revision? We need not be revolutionary in the sense of discarding that which has worked well in the past, but I suggest there are some guide posts to necessary change. First and simplest, we should discard the obsolete and meaningless sections in the constitution. They were transitional in 1867 and are meaningless today. At least 50 sections of the British North America Act could be eliminated.
Second, I believe we need a new preamble to the constitution, and it ought to refer to the historic partnership of English and French speaking people and the contributions of Canadians of other ethnic origins. It ought to make clear that the foundation of our system of government is respect for individual and minority rights, the protection of historic
May 15, 1967	COMMONS
rights of religion, education and language, and a legislative system based on the British parliamentary model. In my view such a preamble would not be mere rhetoric but would be of very definite educational value not only for school children but for the many thousands of immigrants that we expect to welcome to Canada from all over the world.
We ought to entrench in our constitution a constitutional bill of rights. We have at present a bill of rights which was passed by parliament, but its inadequacy is obvious. It does not apply to provincial legislatures, and may be repealed by parliament at any time parliament chooses to legislate in a manner inconsistent with it. According to our courts it has no effect on existing federal legislation. A constitutional bill of rights would be valuable for the defence of our traditional liberties and a useful educational tool to set out explicitly some of our fundamental institutions.
I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say that he will discuss a constitutional bill of rights next month with the premiers of the various provinces. I hope the proposed constitutional amendments incorporating the bill of rights will be made available for discussion in this house before, not after, they are submitted to the provincial authorities.
The core of the constitutional problem is the distribution of legislation power between federal and provincial authorities which is embodied in sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. I think these two sections ought to be reviewed with two aims in mind. First we ought to consider what are the necessary and characteristic functions of modern government in the second half of the twentieth century; also, how are those functions to be allocated between federal and provincial authorities and how are resources to be allocated to enable alloted functions to be efficiently fulfilled. The other point to be borne in mind is whether it is wise, in our revised constitution, or necessary to allow Quebec a special status. The expression "special status" is very general, and it is necessary to be precise when dealing with it. I propose later in my remarks to define more precisely what we in this party mean when we say we are in favour of a special status for Quebec.
Nearly all governments in modern industrial communities, irrespective of ideological background, have been forced into assuming functions quite different from the traditional functions of government. The scourge of unemployment in the '30's has lead to the
DEBATES	203
The Address-Mr. Brewin adoption of Keynesian theories that the government must maintain full employment. This is as true of the United States, which emphasizes its devotion to private enterprise, as it is of various Scandinavian countries that have accepted the philosophy of democratic socialism. Both have moved toward a mixed economy, a sort of partnership between government and private enterprise. Full employment policies, in their turn, create a risk of inflation and rising prices. This leads to demands for government action in price control, and on the other side of the coin governments are asked to assume responsibility for economic growth through public investment and selective intervention in the economy.
Exponents of all political faiths, with the exception of a few dinosaurs, have accepted the theory of government intervention in economic planning. These theories were denounced as socialistic a few years ago, but they are now the stock in trade of all parties in modern societies. The problem is to make economic planning work.
Governments have also accepted responsibility in fields of social security. Lastly, governments today are called on to provide services which I like to call the infrastructure of modern living. Here I refer to housing, health, vastly expanded educational services, urban development and redevelopment. Without government intervention in these fields we could not live as we now live in this modern age.
It is necessary to review government functions to see where different levels of government fit. In our view a federal system of government offers distinct political and economic advantages which would disappear if federal authority were undermined in key areas, those advantages including political stability which is necessary to attract foreign capital and to mobilize domestic capital, a stronger political voice and bargaining power in international affairs and international trade, the maintenance of a free trade area from coast to coast, and a bulwark against foreign domination.
To this end we believe that federal authority must be preserved in such fields as credit, banking, investment, monetary and fiscal policy, tariffs and transportation, to name a few only. There is no room here for special status for Quebec or any province. We have been concerned about the gradual erosion of federal powers in the fields I mentioned which has become apparent in federal-provincial conferences over the past few years.
May 15, 1967

The Address-Mr. Brewin
The responsibilities of various government levels in fields of social security must be clear, that those responsibilities may be ade-quatey discharged. It is desirabe to have federal control in fields such as family allowances, non-contributory old age pensions and the like. There are some fields such as hospitalization and health services where the present system of provincial administration and partial federal financing works well, and where it should be retained with great advantage in transferability of benefits throughout Canada. Here also the federal contribution helps equalize the burden as between provinces.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
In other fields of social security provincial governments, being closer to the people, should have sole responsibility. But if we are to make progress toward the goal of regional equality, equalization payments from the federal treasury will continue to be required. In the field of social security, while a clear allocation of authority is required, I can see no urgent need for a special status for Quebec.
It is in the third field of the collective services or infrastructure, as I have called it, that a special status for Quebec is called for. Quebec does have an historic tradition, culture and language of her own, of which she is justly proud and which she proposed to develop on her own lines. Undoubtedly connected with this fact of cultural difference is the whole field of education at all levels and the development of urban services. If Quebec desires to do these things alone, why not? But if the other nine provinces believe that university education, adult retraining and urban development can be more efficiently planned and financed through the intervention of the federal authority, why should they be held back by the desire of Quebec to be on her own in these matters?
The special status for Quebec which we in this party advocate is not some sort of political concession made to win the political approval of voters in the province of Quebec; it is merely a recognition of the facts of life, namely that people with a special culture of their own are entitled to retain complete control, if they so desire, over matters intimately connected with that culture such as education. On the other hand it must be recognized that it is the people in the other nine provinces who ought to be most insistent that Quebec should have a special status and that federal intervention should not be restricted to the level desired by Quebec.

If I understand the doctrine propounded by the Minister of Justice it is that the present constitutional arrangement, interpreted in such a way that the federal government should stay strictly out of the fields of provincial jurisdiction, is quite sufficient to satisfy the aspirations of the province of Quebec. I do not know whether this is so. However it may be, there is no reason why this doctrine should be accepted by the rest of Canada. There may well be fields of action in which federal intervention is desired by the other provinces although unacceptable to Quebec. If so, the device of a special status for Quebec can be used to meet the aspirations of Quebec on the one hand and the rest of Canada on the other. I am afraid I have no time to give illustrations showing how this would apply.
It appears to me that in this whole field of constitutional reform the government has lamentably failed to give leadership. This is clearly demonstrated by the words put into the mouth of the Governor General in the speech from the throne. This Liberal government was elected four years ago. We have been in a constitutional crisis throughout this whole period. The necessity of taking a look at the constitution has been urged on the government by many different people including many members of this house.
The government, we are told in the speech from the throne, "is aware of its unique responsibility to assure that our fundamental law is readily adaptable to our changing social needs". It is so fully aware of this that after four years in office the best that can be said on the subject is contained in the following phrase: "Studies to obtain the best advice on this important matter are now under way with a view to specific consideration of the whole problem by parliament".
Who will compose this anonymous committee? When will they report? We are told nothing.
What an extraordinary neglect is admitted in these words. The government is so aware of its unique responsibility that now, after four years of constitutional crisis, it is apparently starting to study the subject of constitutional change.
The initiative has passed to provincial governments which are setting up committees, calling conferences and so on. But there is a reason for this federal neglect by the government. The reason is that the government is frightened of parliamentary democracy and is
May 15, 19B7	COMMONS
unwilling to submit to the elected representatives of the various parties the urgent problem of the future constitution of Canada.
The view of the government is described inelegantly as the can of worms theory or the theory of Pandora's box. It is feared that if there is open discussion of our constitutional future excessive demands may be made, and the desire to make political capital will prevail over a sense of responsibility. It is thought that discussion by the members of parliament will add to the difficulties and create disunity rather than consensus. I have no doubt this is the reason the government has failed to set up a parliamentary committee to discuss the future constitution of Canada.
In my view this is a tragic underestimate of the sense of responsibility of members of parliament. It is my opinion that Canadians are capable generally, and elected Canadians are especially capable if they are given the opportunity, of getting down to the difficult but by no means hopeless task of solving their constitutional problems.
As I understand it, it was the practical politicians who laid the basis for confederation at a time when the divisions and distances in Canada were much greater than they are today. This house is representative, as no other group of people can be, of the people of Canada as a whole. We represent every region of Canada; we represent nearly all the politically significant viewpoints of Canadians. We represent practical political views vital to the solution of these problems.
It will be a grave disservice to the future of this country if the present lack of leadership continues. It is, of course, possible to exaggerate the importance of written documents. The unity of Canada does not depend on merely constitutional solutions. It depends upon a modest pride among Canadians; it depends upon good sense and patience. It also depends upon a willingness to tackle problems rather than shove them under the table.
The need for revision of the constitution is one of the most urgent tasks which face this country. We do not need constitutional revolution but we do need constitutional revision and we ought to be getting on with the job. We in this party entirely agree with the opening statement in the motion by the Leader of the Opposition, namely that this house regrets that Her Majesty's advisers have failed to submit any program to give effective direction with regard to Canada's constitutional development in this centennial year. But we
DEBATES	205
The Address-Mr. Brewin do not believe that the calling of a constitutional conference at this stage would be useful. Such a conference, in order to prove fruitful, must be preceded by a great deal of study in this parliament and by a statement of the federal position. A conference called without a background of firm federal preparation could turn into a fiasco and be of little help. I was interested to see that in the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition there was no indication of the direction in which change should take place, no guidance as to the stand the federal authority might take.
I should like to refer now to the subamendment introduced by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). We are frankly at a loss to understand what this amendment means. It was perhaps the product of a great deal of procedural ingenuity so as to fit it within the framework of the rules. We are, of course, very much concerned about the present day difficulties of dairy farmers. We have clear views as to the policies required in order to deal with those difficulties. But the subamendment refers to some sort of constitutional change or amendment-it is very vague-and it does not seem to us to have any bearing whatever on the present problems of dairy farmers or any other farmers, for that matter. We believe in the general statement of concern that is expressed in the amendment, but again we do not think it produces any sort of remedy which to us seems to make any particular sense and therefore we will not be able to support it.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
In conclusion may I say that to many people a discussion of constitutional issues is a tedious and boring matter which they like to leave to constitutional lawyers. I believe, however, that it is one of the most practical and important matters which face us. I believe our workers and our farmers, all our people, can be aided in their search for a better life if we in this house, in parliament and in public life, tackle the problem of a careful thoughtful revision of our constitution. I think it would be wrong for any of us to attempt to lay down hard and fast prescriptions as to precisely what changes we think are necessary. I have outlined some of the changes which we in this party think are necessary. I call on the government to do what it heretofore has failed to do and start to give the needed leadership to the people of Canada.

The Address-Mr. Roxburgh Am I right in thinking that special status as he defines it implies no change in the present constitutional situation toward a further decentralization in favour of Quebec particularly?

I think that whether or not we give a special status there is plenty of room for a process of decentralization, particularly decentralization of federal intervention. I believe this is desirable, but I do not think that meets the problem of whether there is a special status required in such matters as education and perhaps urban renewal, to take two examples.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

speechtext: Special status, the way the hon. member for Greenwood understands it, would seem to me to mean a special status in relation to changes which the hon. member would like to see brought about in the constitutional system. It seems to imply that the special status itself is only the constitutional status quo, as it exists now.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not think so. As I said, one of the big difficulties is that we use expressions like "associated state", "special status" and so on which may mean many different things. Many people say that there already is in the B.N.A. Act a special status for Quebec which recognizes the historic fact of a different culture. All we are saying is that in the expanding function of government we believe there are some things which the province of Quebec might want to do alone and therefore should be exempt from federal jurisdiction but that the other provinces which may want to do these things together under federal jurisdiction should not be held back because legitimately and properly the province of Quebec says that this is something which affects its culture and therefore it wishes to retain control over it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to extend my sincere congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think we all agree that their speeches were of a very high standard. At this time I should also like to pass on my sincere sympathy to the family of Mrs. Ko-nantz, one who was truly loved and respected by all members of this house.
The day following the speech from the throne one of our leading daily papers summarized it in this way: "Something for everyone". I am very sorry to say that one type of

business was not mentioned in the speech from the throne, one which plays a very important part in the economy of this nation. This type of business has also not been mentioned in many throne speeches in the past. I have in mind small business. Often we are led to wonder whether small business, like the small farm, is on its way out. There is certainly little doubt that small business is having one of the toughest times it has ever had to survive, and the cause is not solely competition from large corporations as many people seem to think. There are many other factors and I will deal with them separately.
There still is and must be a place for small business. Except via the small business route where else can an individual with the desire, the initiative, and of course always with a limited amount of financing, start. Be it industrial, retail, farming or fishing, it is all small business. Many of the large corporate business of today had their start in this very medium. As a member of the government party I almost hate to say this in the House of Commons, but while checking not with one but with many small businessmen not only in my own constituency but elsewhere in the province of Ontario and in other provinces throughout Canada I found that the one main factor that is working against small business is the autocratic bureaucracy of all governments in legislating their new way of life. It is a good life and it is all right to have such legislation, but by the time the small businessman meets the demands in respect of all the social and other benefits of government there is little left for his efforts. These efforts are not completed in an eight hour day or a five day week. They extend anywhere from 12 to 14 or 15 hours a day and in many many cases for seven days a week. The corporate business is better able to cope with the current trend since it is better equipped, better staffed and of course has greater financial stability than the struggling merchant or small industry.
A recent report of the Department of Finance pointed out that the steady decline of net income of non-farm, non-incorporated businesses from 8.5 per cent in 1949 to 5.5 per cent in 1965 continued downward to 5.1 per cent in the first half of 1966. I should like to point out that this drop in profit would appear to be exceeded only by farm operators, who represent another form of small business.
While talking to different businessmen throughout my constituency and in other parts of the country, a local small businessman pointed out to me recently that many
May IS, 1967	COMMONS
small businesses are acting as a training ground, which they can ill afford to do, tor employees who are being taken by larger businesses. Many of these small businesses have spent a year or more training employees in the managerial aspect of their businesses only to have them grabbed up by big business. The experience gained by employees in small businesses enables them to obtain better positions at the expense of the small businessman. Small businessmen realize that this is part of the game they must play and they accept the fact, but this is an illustration of one of the additional problems the small businessman must face.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I am sure that the government wants to do something for these people operating small private enterprises, but the truth of the matter is, I am sorry to say, that the government does not realize their true plight. The local merchant to whom I referred suggested that wages and other benefits for labour are increasing. He suggests there is nothing wrong in this regard but feels that the government should direct some attention to the rather rocky road being travelled by those who wish to succeed in small private enterprises. Have we thought about these small businessmen who make up the heart of our economy? These are people who are ambitious to the extent they will work longer than a five day week or an eight hour day. If the efforts of these enterprising Canadians are to be curtailed by an overbearing bureaucracy then this nation will be brought to stagnation by two classes of people, those who want shorter working hours and those who are resting comfortably at the top of the business ladder. Surely this country does not want to see that happen.
In the majority of cases small businesses are family businesses, and I include in this category small farms and fishing operations. People in this category are becoming very disturbed about the fact that these are the only types of corporate enterprises not able to employ wives, pay them a salary and deduct their wages at the end of the year as a business expense as other corporate businesses are allowed to do. This creates an extreme hardship on the small businessman. Large industrial concerns are not particularly concerned about employing wives but many enterprises take advantage of the fact that the salary of wives can be deducted as a business expense. This leaves only the small businessman and the professional man as exceptions
DEBATES	207
The Address-Mr. Roxburgh to the general rule applying to incorporated businesses.
In many cases the professional man is not interested in whether his wife works, but the small businessman often has to employ his wife in an effort to succeed. In this case the wife takes a greater interest in the business than an ordinary employee and puts in longer hours when the husband is away on business such as buying trips. However, at income tax time her efforts in helping to maintain the community enterprise are not rewarded as are the efforts of her counterpart in many other cases.
We as members of parliament must realize that there are valid reasons that no changes have been made in the act in this regard. However, we must realize that with the continuing trend toward amalgamation some thought should be given to easing the income tax restrictions regarding the part wives play in the successful operation of small businesses. I hope the government will give sincere and serious consideration to easing the restrictions in this regard.
When talking to these small businessmen one hears a great many different stories, but I should like to give one factual illustration of the discrimination which takes place. One young retail merchant I know lost his top employee not many months ago to a franchise grocery chain. As a result his wife had to increase her number of working hours until a replacement was found. That happened two months ago and a replacement has not yet been found. This is a young family with small children and a part-time housekeeper had to be hired to look after the needs of the children. Had this family been in a position to hire a full-time housekeeper they could deduct this expense as a business item. The family was not in a position to do so and as a result cannot classify the housekeeper's wages as a business expense. Something is wrong with our system when some sort of adjustment cannot be made to help small businessmen under these circumstances.
Originally under the Small Businesses Loans Act the government guaranteed chartered bank loans to small enterprises engaged in manufacturing, wholesaling or retailing or service industries to a maximum of $25,000. These loans must be secured and may be repaid over a period of up to ten years with an interest rate of 5J per cent. One might think these people could go to the bank and easily obtain a loan but nothing could be further from the truth in the past few years. I
May 15. 1967

The Address-Mr. Roxburgh know of dozens of small businessmen who have not been able to get a loan from a chartered bank under any circumstances. Many of them were advised by bankers to try to obtain a loan somewhere else because of all the red tape involved. I am not suggesting something that is not factual. The banker who gave me this information told me that from the time a small businessman made his application to the time he received the loan from the bank he would forget what he wanted it for. Let us face the facts. In plain language, during the past few years at least -I am not going into the future but am talking about the past-the banks were just not interested in making loans to small businesses. Let nobody, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), suggest that they were, because they were not.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Under a recent revision of the Small Businesses Loans Act by the Department of Finance, companies in construction, transportation and communications will qualify for small business loans for the first time. The maximum gross revenue of companies eligible for loans has been doubled from $250,000 to $500,000. This should benefit particularly small trading firms whose profits are at a low percentage. The interest rate is, of course, 5J per cent as before.
It may be asked, what is the difference now? The difference is found in the atmosphere created by the changes in the Bank Act. With interest rates dropping and the prevailing rate holding at about 6 per cent it is now felt that, having regard to the 5i per cent guaranteed by the government of Canada and the 6 per cent charged by the banks, a difference of only half of 1 per cent, the banks will now be more generous in lending money to small businesses. We hope this will be so.
Everything nowadays points to expansion in business, in farming and every other line of industry, the thought being, of course, that the larger the unit the more economic it is to handle. That is all very fine, but let me say now that bigness in business is possibly getting a little too big, and its coming is doing away with incentives to the average individual who does not want to become just another link in a chain that is putting incentives in the hands of a very few. Let us not forget that when an individual loses desire because of little or no incentive it is not only bad for the individual but for the community and the country in which he lives.

I do not think the good old opposition on the other side of the chamber will disagree that the economy of the country has never been better than at the present time. But-here is that great word "but"; if it were not in our language I do not know what we would do-what will happen if the economy of the country should slacken off rather drastically? No one will ever want to see a return of the conditions of the 1930's, no matter what party forms the government. But who is to say this is not possible? The thinking now, as we hear it from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and other people, is to the effect that the future will see a guaranteed average income for the people of Canada. That is fine. I only hope it will prove to be true. We all hope it will prove to be true. But as the Prime Minister very forcibly pointed out, this can only be accomplished if the economy of the country is kept at a very high level.
May I, as a very ordinary backbencher who has had the privilege of being in this house for at least three sessions, give this little warning. A friend of mine said that backbenchers do not have much say in this house. That is wrong, because we do. There is no argument about this; the proof of the pudding is in the eating. But let me issue this little warning. No matter what we do in Canada to promote our economy, a country such as ours which depends so much on its exports-the Kennedy round of negotiation is just finishing-in order to keep its economy sound can only be as financially sound as the nations with which it deals. If we had to export only 10 per cent of what we produce in this country, that would be different. In other words, the future economy of Canada depends upon the future economy of the countries of the world.
I would like somebody to answer this question before I conclude. What happened to large business and industry in the 1930's? What would happen to large business now if there were a sudden drop in the country's economy? I believe that any person in business knows that many businesses are existing on a very marginal profit at the present time. I would like to deal with the situation in the 1930's because there are many young people in parliament and the young people will be running our country in the future. They have the education to enable them to do this but they have not had the experience of the 1930's. Very often it is a good thing to have had experience. Nobody can deny that big business crashed in the 1930's, taking thousands of large and small investors with it
May 15, 1967	COMMONS
as well as the workers in those industries. What happened to small business in the 1930's? Small business carried the load and managed to survive and those that did not survive hurt but a few.
Before the 1930's it was my privilege to work on a large ranch in the Okanagan. I am very sorry that some of my good western friends and those from the prairies are not in the house at the moment. It may be difficult for people to believe, and even more difficult for me to believe now, that I actually hitched up and drove eight horses at a time. I worked on a very large ranch of thousands of acres. While there I made a friend who had a 25-acre fruit farm. Before the 1930's he was doing well. Mrs. Roxburgh and I had the privilege of going back there a number of times during the 1930's and later. During the 1930's my friend with his small, 25-acre fruit farm, his Chinese cook and very limited help during harvest, was able to make a small profit. That small profit was enough to allow him to go south for a couple of months during the winter.
There were two large ranches in the area. What happened to them? I will not mention any names in this connection. The two large fruit, grain and cattle ranches of a few thousand acres in size, which had been doing nicely before the 1930's, lost money and had to sell packets of land of 25 to 50 acres to people coming in from the midwest so the owners could pay their water rates and taxes. My friend with his small business did not have to do that. I understand that eventually one of the larger ranchers went completely bankrupt.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In conclusion I simply say: Let us not be carried away by all this bigness because it can become too big for our good. This government or any other government must somehow make it possible for small business to carry on so that it can not only play its part in the economy of the country but, what is most important as far as I am concerned and I know as far as all hon. members are concerned, provide the opportunities for advancement which it offers to the people of Canada. To keep small business alive is a must.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by congratulating the hon. members for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote), the mover and seconder of the address in reply. I think their speeches were of very high calibre and I
DEBATES	209
The Address-Hon. J. A. MacLean would like to congratulate the mover especially.
I think the throne speech debate should be a free expression of views and ideas by all members of parliament. This should be an occasion when ideas come up from the grass roots to the government rather than the reverse, which is what happens most of the time in a session of parliament when the members of parliament are required to pass judgment on programs which are put before the house by the government. Over the years I have heard many good ideas put forth by private members in various parts of the house in this and other debates of the session. When they were not considered newsworthy, regardless of their merit they seemed to go completely unnoticed and now they exist only in an embalmed state in the tomes of Hansard. Sometimes I think there should be some sort of group, either composed of members of the press or perhaps of members of the research branch of the parliamentary library, which might prepare a digest of the debates so that the public could receive in capsule form information about what the members of parliament are thinking and speaking about because, generally speaking, the public seems to think that members of parliament are mainly engaged in squabbling with each other and that they never come up with anything that is really constructive.
This is our centennial year and I believe we should attempt to look not just one year ahead, as we usually do at the opening of a normal session of parliament, but to look ahead at a whole century. We will not be very successful in doing this but the mental gymnastics involved will at least be helpful, I think. That being the case, of course, we will only be able to look at the high spots of these very greatly widened horizons and the details will have to be examined at some other time.
Members of parliament usually speak as representatives of their constituents and their constituents are considered to be the only people they represent. I think this was probably true to a large extent 100 years ago but owing to the fact that the world is shrinking members of parliament, elected representatives and leaders in all fields are becoming more and more the representatives of a greatly widened constituency. They are becoming the representatives of the whole of mankind. What we do or fail to do may well in the future determine the success or failure of the whole of humanity.
May 15, 1967

The Address-Hon. J. A. MacLean
If I were to choose a theme for the rambling remarks I intend to make perhaps I would suggest that it be terre des hommes, man and his world, which is the theme of Expo '67. I realize that I am running a great danger here because the title of the book which gave its theme to Expo was translated into English as "Wind, Sand and Stars". It might be said of my remarks that I intended to make a windy speech throwing sand in the eyes of my opponents so that they would see stars. However, I should like to point out that this is not my intention because in this book the wind is the wind of the spirit, the sand is the earth from which we sprang and which gives us sustenance, and the stars are our place in the cosmos.
My interpretation of the theme "man and his world" bears absolutely no relationship to the one given by Expo, but I should like to say that man's relationship to the world has changed rapidly over a relatively short period of time. In the days of the Greeks and the Romans, the civilizations from which most of what we cherish has sprung, the known world was a very limited area around the Mediterranean sea and everything beyond that was terra incognita. It was the unknown world. But as time progressed and Marco Polo and others made contact with other civilizations in other parts of the world, man's horizons began to widen. Later came the marvelous era of discovery across the oceans. Nevertheless during this period the thoughts of men were governed by the fact that, as Aristotle said, the earth was the centre of creation and everything revolved around it.
About 300 years ago a new, revolutionary and earth-shaking philosophy was put forward by the astronomers of the day who were made to suffer for their views. Galileo, Brunnow and Copernicus put forward the shocking suggestion that perhaps the world was not the centre of everything and that we, the little egocentric beings, were not the most important or the whole of God's creation. Then, as men's vision began to widen they saw that their place in the universe was not as great as they had previously supposed. With the aid of telescopes men perceived the grandeur of the constellations. They began to realize that space was a vast extent. They believed, however, that the sun was the centre of creation and the planets revolved about it. The other stars were of no significance.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
With the building of bigger and bigger telescopes developed by amateurs like Herschel

they began to realize the magnitude of creation. In a paper which he read to the Royal Society in 1785 on the construction of the heavens Herschel, who professionally was an organist in Bath, England, explained why he found it necessary to build larger telescopes. He stated that to the unaided eye the milky way appears as a diffuse band of light across the sky. Through a small telescope it seems to be a collection of stars but many nebulous patches remain unresolved. Herschel said that as the power of the telescope is increased an observer perceives that those objects which had been called nebulae are evidently nothing but clusters of stars. He finds their numbers increase upon him, and when he resolves one nebula into stars he discovers ten new ones which he cannot resolve.
The British astronomer, Professor Lovell, points out the difficulty encountered by the mind of man in resolving his insignificant place in creation. He said that the egocentric idea was so firmly embedded in men's minds that even after the acceptance of the motion of the earth and the planets around the sun it was still believed that the solar system was in the centre of the universe of fixed stars. He says he was brought up on the idea that the sun was in the centre of a stellar system of many millions of stars distributed throughout such a volume of space that light would take
20.000	years to traverse the universe. Then he goes on to say that in later years he realized that we are not only cosmically small but we are in a rather undignified position amongst the stars of the milky way.
I should interject here, Mr. Speaker, that occasionally since I have been a member of parliament I have tried to make the odd speech which would expand our view and look at things in perhaps a philosophical light. Like most speeches of that type, they went completely unnoticed. As I have said, they are embalmed in the tomes of Hansard. Once in a while I am moved to make another just to keep them company. This introduction to my remarks merely serves to point out that in the last 100 years there has been a tremendous expansion of imagination, of thought and of understanding of our world. We have to rise to the occasion to assess and understand the significance of our world better than we did in the past. We know now that our galaxy is only one of millions of galaxies in the universe. Our galaxy, which is the milky way, is so large that it takes light about
100.000	years to cross it from side to side. However, it is minute compared with the whole of the universe.
May 15, 1967	COMMONS
As a matter of fact, galaxies like ours are so numerous in the heavens that they are counted in the thousands of millions. With the modern equipment which has recently been developed it is possible to locate and measure these galaxies out in space. The Harvard observatory has become so efficient in this operation that they are able to locate and chart new galaxies as large as ours at a cost of about $52 a hundred. However, each of these galaxies contains up to thousands of millions of stars, each one as significant as our sun.
As a result of world war II there have been tremendous advances in man's understanding of the environment in which he lives. This has been brought about chiefly by three things. The first was the putting into operation of the 200-inch optical telescope at Palomar in California, then the development of radio-astronomy, and finally the artificial earth satellites. We have now reached the place where we can probe into space a distance of about 6,000 million light years. A light year, of course, is the distance that light will travel at a rate of 186,000 miles a second in a year. However, the expanse of the universe is so vast we can no longer assume we are alone. Even if we assumed that the chances of a star like our sun having in its orbit another earth like ours that would be suitable for life were only one in a million, there would still be hundreds of millions of places where life probably exists.
How do we shore up our ego when we realize we are no longer the centre of creation and that we are only a recent phenomenon? We have not proven our ability to survive. We can create no impression of significance as a result of size or anything of that sort. This probably makes us feel rather humble and insignificant. When men believed they were the centre of everything, the centre of creation, a certain type of piety was very common. It still exists, even amongst members of this house. I can think of one case in the group to my left and one amongst the government of a very strong sense of piety, but it is a piety that stems from a reverence for the supreme being based upon his supposed resemblance to themselves. This idea is no longer enough for us. We must find some other reason to give meaning to the fact that we exist.

In a century, Canada as a people and territory will become part of a solitary nation, or a new world of few nations.
