But I think many of us can rise above regionalism and parochialism, see both sides of the question, understand each other and draw closer together. It is most regrettable that we continually read in newspapers that this or that province will separate from our confederation. Canada is a great nation. We can work together, we have to work together as we have in the past, and in that way we can overcome this narrow parochialism and regionalism.
We in the House of Commons fight about language. Let us look at some of the statistics of language. If we consider the population of North America we find that 80 million people on this continent speak Spanish. The statistics show that approximately 250 million people today speak English, and 25 per cent of the world's population speak some form of Chinese. If we are really concerned about the problem perhaps we should be learning to speak Chinese so we may understand these people, because it is in free intercourse one with the other that we will bring about understanding, particularly at a time when we are talking about international crises. Of the world population 8.3 per cent speak Russian. Seventy per cent of all the letters written in the world are written in English.
I do not know why we spend so much time arguing about language. I appreciate anybody speaking in another tongue. I wish I had had the opportunity as a young man in my formal education to learn many languages. I wish that when I went to school I had had the
May 15, 1967

opportunity, like other members of my family, to learn two or three languages. I think it is wonderful to understand languages. But why spend so much time on and be supersensitive about whether something is written in French, Spanish or English? What does it matter? This narrow regionalism and parochialism is eroding and sapping the very spirit of the nation.
I now wish to turn to another subject with which I think any government should come to grips. I want to come to grips with the question of the expropriation of land in this nation. As counsel I have had some experience with expropriation law and expropriation cases. I have also been most active, as a member of parliament, in the northern affairs committee since coming to the House of Commons. The reason I have been so interested in this matter is, I suppose, that I have had the privilege, opportunity and indeed the honour of representing Banff National Park, one of the beauty spots of North America.
We talk about civil rights. I am not pointing an accusing finger at the present government when making this speech because the abuses in expropriation to which I will draw attention have occurred in every province under provincial law and federal law. The abuses that have occurred under federal law are the worst of all. I hope that the speech I make today will have some impact in solving this problem for those who are in the chamber and those who may read my speech later. The Bill of Rights is involved in this problem. Let us look at the Canadian Bill of Rights. I have always felt it to be most regrettable that the courts have refused to give effect to the Bill of Rights. They refuse to give it meaning and significance. Perhaps the courts believe the Bill of Rights is not a constitutional change, but it is pretty definite in some of its language and it was approved by parliament. The Canadian Bill of Rights provides:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely-
What are they?
-the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;
When I talk about the expropriation of land I shall deal with civil rights in the enjoyment of property. The right to own property in this nation is a civil right. That right should not

The Address-Mr. Woolliams be taken away from the individual without due process of law as set out in the Bill of Rights. With all due respect to the Bill of Rights, I might go so far as to say that this was the law before the Bill of Rights was enacted.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
What is the federal authority in respect of expropriation? It has the authority and must have the authority to expropriate land for public works. It has to have the authority to expropriate land for a railway. People cannot be allowed to stop the development of the nation. It also has to have the authority to expropriate land for national parks under certain circumstances. I will have more to say about that later.
The next question I ask is, how does expropriation in Canada operate under our laws? Let us take the case of the national parks. The officials of the public works department get together and prepare an order in council with a description of the land. When it is drawn up it is then approved by the executive. The order in council is then filed in the land titles office. That is how it is started. No notice is given to the owners. I can show hon. members hundreds of cases where no notice has been given. In fact, in the case of national parks it has been a deliberate policy of the department not to give notice of expropriation.
In one of the cases before the Exchequer Court in which I acted as counsel no notice was given to three men who were pioneers of western Canada. Their land was taken away from them, and even under cross-examination we have been unable to find out the reason for this action. However, the cat came out of the bag in an examination for discovery, and the case has just been completed so I can discuss it here. It is the case of Lake Louise Ski Lodge Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen involving three people who owned 60 acres of land of which the pivotal point is Lake Louise. Today multimillion dollar enterprises, including a visitors' centre, are being built there by the government, which had some trouble in negotiating a financial agreement in expropriating land for the trans-Canada highway. All the government needed at that time was four to five acres of land for the roads, but when I cross-examined the officials they told me they could not complete the kind of deal they wanted and the price for the four
May 15. 1967

The Address-Mr. Woolliams or five acres was not right. I asked the director of the national parks what was his answer to that, and he replied:
Such action did not appear necessary at that time if the land for the right-of-way could have been acquired for a reasonable amount.
Then I asked him:
So that it was really, then, the result that as you were not able to negotiate for the highway that you did actually expropriate the other land?
To which he answered "yes". In other words, 55 or 56 acres were taken over for the sake of four or five acres. Surely this is not taking over land under due process of law.
Of course the right to expropriate could be challenged, but who can afford this legal procedure? Let us consider what happens after the land is expropriated, and this is the worst part. The onus is then on the owners to try to negotiate with the department of the government, and if they cannot reach an agreement they must start an action in the Exchequer Court of Canada. This means that an owner, who may be a man with very limited means, must hire a good lawyer because one cannot go to the Exchequer Court without a lawyer with a good deal of skill. It is also necessary to hire a top appraiser, which is costly. In the Lake Louise case the judgment given by the Exchequer Court was about $96,000.
The original letter offered these people $13,000 for the land, so they had to hire a lawyer. They had to get appraisers and engineers. This does not sound like much, but before you can place your case before the Exchequer Court you have to allow about $20,000 without even considering a dollar for your lawyer or for experts to assist you.
I say that the law in this regard is wrong. I realize that to run the country efficiently land is needed for parks, highways and railways. Individuals cannot be allowed to hold up the development and progress of the nation. However, I say that the expropriation law is being spelled out by certain officials of the department so as to make it work for them and not the owner. I believe the law should be changed so that if negotiations are unsuccessful the crown should start the action. A time limit should be set for the negotiations, after which the crown must start an action. The crown should carry the ball and the onus should be on it to prove what the land is worth. The owner should then take the defence. Today the onus is on the owner of the land. Under the Bill of Rights no one should lose the enjoyment of his property without due process of the law.

Today if an owner is financially crippled and his property is expropriated he cannot get justice because he cannot afford to buy it.
Let us take a look at another situation where leases are being taken over in the national parks. No one on the government side has raised a voice in protest. It is a most shocking situation. The reason may be that there is no national park in Ontario or Quebec. There are land ownerships in fee simple. Leases in perpetuity were granted years ago and this is almost the same as a title in fee simple. Then there are 99-year leases and 4 2-year leases with the right to renew for 21 years. The department has denied this. The officials say that this cannot happen. But it does happen. A parliamentary committee met in Banff, and at that time the national parks branch filed a big yellow bible on their policies. I did a little homework that night and I found something which I should like to put on the record. I am referring to the advice of the Department of Justice given to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing). It reads as follows:
On normal renewals of perpetual renewal leases, the department can probably be forced (legally) to issue renewal leases also containing the perpetual renewal clauses... on a normal renewal of a perpetual renewal lease we cannot legally force the lessee to take only a 42- or a 42 plus 21-year lease in its stead.
In spite of this advice what did the minister do? I have hundreds of letters on file, but here is one from someone in Jasper. I will not give his name because that might cause his ruination. He was told that the department would approve the registration of his mortgage for the building provided he gave up his lease in perpetuity to the crown and in return took a 42-year lease. I say that this is blackmail. This would be considered duress under any law. The crown in the name of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is guilty of this sort of thing. It is going on continually.
I have already spoken about the difficulties involved in placing an expropriation case before the Exchequer Court. I put the following simple question on the order paper:
Will the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development take the appropriate action to have referred, pursuant to the provisions of section 55 of the Supreme Court Act, to the Supreme Court of Canada, the questions (a) whether the so-called perpetual leases in the national parks were legally granted by the Crown-
The officers of the crown swore before the committee that these leases were legally
May 15. 1967	COMMONS
granted. They said they would have to renew them under the present terms and conditions. The minister and his department say they will not allow a person to build or will not approve the mortgage unless he gives up what he has and accepts less in return.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I asked that question and what kind of answer did I get? It was an amazing answer. The officials stayed up all night so I would not get the facts. I asked the government to take the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada and this is the answer I received:
I am advised with respect to so-called perpetually renewable leases granted by the minister of the interior prior to the enactment of the National Parks Act in 1930, that the minister of the interior did not have the power to grant a right of renewal in those terms and therefore that portion of the leases was ultra vires his power and authority-
I asked the government it they would refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada to ascertain whether or not the leases were legal. They said they were not legal. Why do I want the government to take up the matter with the Supreme Court of Canada? I desire this because it costs a citizen so much money to go before the Exchequer Court. Where does the Exchequer Court sit, Mr. Speaker? It sits in Ottawa but will go to other places. Every time there is a procedural question it has to be argued in Ottawa. No citizen can afford, unless he is a wealthy man, to become involved in a lawsuit in the Exchequer Court of Canada. May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REPORT ON RESULTS OF GENEVA TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, almost 50 countries accounting for 80 per cent of the world's trade have for some four years now been negotiating the Kennedy round of trade expansion at Geneva under the provisions of 27053-15
DEBATES	221
Report on Geneva Tariff Negotiations GATT. Basic agreement among major trading countries was reached about an hour ago in Geneva. There is about $40 billion worth of trade in products in which concessions have been made.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) joined me in Geneva last Thursday and we participated with our delegation in the last critical stages when crucial decisions were necessary. During that time we had policy discussions with representatives of our important trading partners, the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, the Common Market, the group of Nordic countries and Australia. With some heads of delegations we had more than one meeting. I also met on several occasions with Mr. Eric Wyndam White, director general of GATT, the organization under whose auspices these important trade negotiations have been held. He has been a tower of strength and we all owe him a debt of gratitude for his contributions to world trade.
I believe these talks made a constructive contribution to negotiations, both from a general viewpoint and particularly in terms of Canadian trading interests. Many of the final points revolved around agriculture, and it was both opportune and helpful to have the Minister of Agriculture with me.
From the Canadian point of view, concessions which have been negotiated in foreign markets represent the most important trade pact in this century and affect some billions of dollars of trade. From a world point of view, negotiations have achieved a most important advance in lowering tariff and other barriers to trade.
For example, in the United States tariffs have been reduced or completely eliminated on $1 billion to $1.5 billion of Canadian goods moving into that market. Also the lowering of tariffs should make it possible to sell goods we have not previously been able to merchandise there. In this market we have gained markedly improved access over a very extensive range of products which will be of great benefit to our industry, our agriculture, our fisheries and to our industrial development generally.
In addition to making substantial tariff reductions over many thousands of items, the United States has agreed to eliminate its tariffs on a large number of Canadian products. These tariff cuts will greatly enhance our export prospects, and I know that our exporters will take full advantage of all these possibilities which will become progressively
May 15, 1967

Report on Geneva Tariff Negotiations available over a period of five years, starting January 1, 1968.
Reductions to be made in Canadian tariff as part of these reciprocal arrangements will be of benefit to Canadian consumers and to users of a wide variety of imported products. This will help reduce costs of production for our farms, fisheries, mines and industry. But to make our way in a more competitive world, we will have to be alert to opportunities that are presented. To take full advantage of these changes, our businessmen, our workers, our farmers and, indeed, all Canadians will have to accept the reality of a more competitive world and make necessary adjustments to reap rewards from this new situation.
While it is not yet possible to make public detailed results because not all GATT countries have, as yet, had the opportunity of agreeing to them, I can say with respect to wheat that the basic elements of a new international wheat arrangement have been agreed between major exporting and importing countries. We have achieved a significant and welcome increase in international minimum and maximum prices for specified qualities of wheat, and substantially strengthened arrangements for co-operation to maintain market stability. For No. 1 Manitoba northern, in store at the lakehead, new minimum and maximum prices will be $1,954 and $2,384 Canadian respectively. This represents about a 21 cent increase over minimum and maximum prices in the current international wheat agreement. Minimum price f.o.b. Vancouver will be $2,034 and maximum $2,464. A growing volume of Canadian wheat is being marketed through this port.
The minimum price agreed upon is $1.73 per bushel for No. 2 hard winter wheat, United States funds, with a quality differential of 224 cents for No. 1 Manitoba northern. Allowing for differentials in freight between gulf ports and lakehead ports, and between United States and Canada currency, this works out to the Canadian figures I have mentioned above.
Agreement has also been reached on a new food aid program totalling some 134 million tons over three years, under which responsibility for providing food assistance to developing countries will be more equitably shared by the member countries of GATT. Canada's share in this program is half a million tons a year. The fact that for the first time industrialized importing countries have agreed to co-operate with wheat producing countries in this joint program represents a

major achievement and an important forward step in international co-operation designed to help meet food needs of the developing world. Canada played a prominent role in the realization of this aim.
During the critical phases of the negotiations on wheat, the Canadian delegation included senior representatives of major producer organizations in western Canada who are members of the public advisers committee of the Canadian Wheat Board. I refer particularly to Messrs. Charles Gibbings, chairman of the advisory committee and president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Roy Atkinson, president of the National Farmers Union, Dr. Bill Parker, president of Manitoba Pool Elevators Limited, Mac Runciman, president of the United Grain Growers Limited, and John Stevens of Morinville, Alberta. Their advice made a most valued contribution to the satisfactory result attained. I am advised that the new price range and other arrangements which have been agreed carry the full support of the public advisers as, of course, they do of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Tariff cuts which have been secured from the United States, the Common Market, Japan and other countries will confer benefits on all sectors and regions of our country. The degree to which this applies depends upon our diligence and skill in pursuing the opportunities they present.
Tariff reductions which Canada and other industrial countries are making will also be of benefit to developing countries of the world. A number of such countries have participated in these negotiations and have offered improved trading opportunities for Canada.
In agriculture, reductions which we have secured in foreign markets over a broad range of products will benefit farmers from coast to coast. Important tariff cuts have been made by other countries in respect of our exports of basic materials, metals and forest products. Major gains have been made through elimination and reduction of tariffs of fish and fisheries products.
Reductions which will be made in industrial tariffs of the United States, E.E.C., and other countries, many on a uniform basis of 50 per cent, will help Canadians to increase both variety and volume of our exports to these markets. Improved access to foreign markets which has been secured should, through expanded exports, significantly help our manufacturers to achieve economies of scale and specialization which are so necessary to improving our efficiency, productivity and competitive position.
May 15, 1967

A new anti-dumping code has been agreed by Canada and our major trading partners, designed to improve existing practices in world trade while safeguarding legitimate interests of our domestic producers.
Benefits for Canada have been secured not only through bilateral negotiations with our most important trading partners but also as a result of indirect benefits which will accrue to Canada from agreements which have been reached between other pairs and groups of countries participating in the Kennedy round. This was an important factor in these successful multilateral negotiations.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Detailed elaboration of agreements which have been reached is now going forward; formal legal documents should be ready for signature before the end of June. Shortly thereafter it is planned that detailed results will be announced simultaneously by all participating countries.
Canada can take great satisfaction that success has crowned efforts which we and others have made over the last four years to conclude this largest ever world trade negotiation started through the initiative and statesmanship of the late President Kennedy.
People, Mr. Speaker, are the essential ingredient in any endeavour, and in this prolonged, sometimes frustrating and most difficult of all trade negotiations, this was the determining factor. Our negotiating team, led by the deputy ministers of the departments concerned, was highly competent, devoted and tireless, often negotiating right through the night.
In the early stages of the Kennedy round our team was led by Mr. Norman Robertson and supported, until recently, by Mr. Hector McKinnon, an experienced veteran of many multilateral trade negotiations. More recently our work at Geneva was guided and coordinated by Mr. Sidney D. Pierce, a distinguished diplomat whose resolute optimism was finally rewarded. It was a matter of comfort to all of us that our ambassador and permanent representative to the European office of the United Nations, Mr. Sol Rae, was always so readily available with help, guidance and encouragement.
On behalf of the government and, I presume, parliament as well I wish to pay tribute and to express our gratitude to all these devoted public servants in whom Canada can be justifiably proud.

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) I am concerned about the second point he raised which was not about goods in general but about wheat. The minister said that he could not tell the house what the situation presently is. I hope we shall not have another automotive pact situation. We shall look forward with interest to what will take place between Canada, the United States and other trading nations. Agreements sometimes look good on paper, as did the automotive agreement, but their reality is not as attractive as the words with which they are painted.
I am glad that the minister mentioned Charles Gibbings, the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, who assisted the government to come to terms on wheat in reference to the world wheat agreement.
Canada is the only nation in the world that exports wheat and does not subsidize its farmers for growing wheat. People in other parts of the country often think that when the farmers receive wheat board payments they receive money from the Canadian treasury. That is false. The wheat board operates as a pool. It receives an initial payment and a second payment which, added together, constitute the pool price and is a price paid the farmer from the sale of his wheat.
It should be understood that the 21 cent increase will apply only to those countries that are signatories to the agreement. Countries such as China and Russia which are outside the agreement will not be affected, except indirectly. We must conclude, that the farmer tonight or tomorrow will not receive an extra 21 cents per bushel for the wheat he delivers to the elevator. That should be understood, and I am glad that the minister did not misrepresent this fact.
As was said some years ago when Britain applied to join the European Common Market, Great Britain over the years has been Canada's best wheat customer. It will be interesting to see if this agreement will affect the price of wheat sold to Great Britain. The farmers well remember when another liberal minister of a Liberal government some years ago promised Great Britain that it could have wheat for $1 per bushel on a five year deal. That promise cost the western farmers $600 million.
The western farmers also remember that in Calgary in 1963 and 1964 the Prime Minister promised the farmers $2 per bushel for No. 1 northern wheat. He did not specify whether
May 15, 1967

Report on Geneva Tariff Negotiations that was the price at the local elevator, the lakehead, Fort William, or Vancouver. Considering that 5 per cent only of western wheat is No. 1 northern, the Prime Minister's promise, even if it had been kept, did not amount to anything.
For years there has been talk of a two-price system. When the Conservative government was in office it considered that Canada consumes approximately 100 million bushels of wheat annually for human and other consumption and the western farmers received a bonus to help them combat the cost-price squeeze. The farmers in 1967 will look at the present situation carefully in the light of recent increases in farm machinery and other agricultural costs. A pusher combine which five or six years ago cost $10,000 now costs the farmers at Rosetown and Kindersley $17,000 to $18,000. The inquiry set up by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) is strangely silent in view of the increasing cost of farm machinery. In fact, farm unions of Saskatchewan and Alberta are boycotting farm machinery companies at this time because of high prices.
The agreement may help farmers somewhat but it will not guarantee all farmers another 21 cents per bushel. Unless farmers can earn more they will not be able to pay the high costs for farm machinery they are presently forced to pay. The farmers today are caught in the worst cost-price squeeze in the history of agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) concerning major changes in tariffs following the meetings now concluded in Geneva will certainly be welcomed by many people in Canada as well as in countries abroad.
At least the Kennedy round of negotiations did not end in complete failure. All the months and years of negotiation did not come to an end without some final conclusion being reached even if it was not wholly satisfactory.
I will say no more about this aspect because, understandably, the minister was unable to give us very much detail as to the way in which the new arrangements will affect specific products important to the export and import markets of Canada.
I turn to the announcement respecting the price of wheat for the next three years. I am sure the minister realizes this will be greeted with a somewhat mixed reaction on the part of farmers in western Canada who produce most of this wheat. It is at least a little encouraging to see that there is to be some increase in price for the next three years. At the same time I believe that the farmers justifiably expected something more than the 21 cents the minister has announced because, as has been pointed out by the two members who spoke immediately prior to me, this certainly does not make up for the increased cost of producing wheat over the years.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) mentioned that the increase is 21 cents over a price that was agreed upon six years ago. I am sure the minister knows very well that a price of slightly over $2 as a maximum is the price at which Canadian wheat farmers have been selling their wheat for about the last 15 years. If this agreement runs at this price to its conclusion on July 31, 1970, this means there will have been an increase of about 10 to 12 per cent over a 15 year period. I am sure there is no other commodity in Canada which has had such a small increase during that period of time. Certainly there is no comparable increase in the cost of anything the farmers buy. The
May IS, 1967

Report on Geneva Tariff Negotiations increase in the cost of the goods the farmers buy has been many times 10 to 12 per cent from 1952 or 1953 up to the present time.
If this trend continues the cost of the things the farmer must buy will continue to rise until the end of this agreement. Increases in wages and increases in incomes in almost all other sectors of the Canadian economy have been substantially-in most cases many times-more than 10 to 12 per cent over this 15 year period. However, as I have said it is at least encouraging to see that there is some increase in the price of wheat because when the negotiations closed in London a few weeks ago the signatory countries to the international wheat agreement could not agree on any price and it appeared there would be some uncertainty in the wheat market for the next three year period. Although, as I say, the increase is not satisfactory in relation to costs, at least there is a small increase.
In so far as Canada's contribution to food aid is concerned, we welcome the announcement that many of the other countries in the western world will now share in a food aid pool that will be of benefit to the countries which from time to time need this kind of support, I suggest that 13-J million tons over a three-year period is a rather significant amount when it is coupled with some of the other aid programs which I am sure many countries will continue quite outside of this agreement. Canada's share seems to be a reasonable amount in this situation.
I would hope the minister would give some consideration to including some wheat flour in our aid because we have in the past supplied the wheat and it has been shipped to other countries for milling and then on to the recipient countries. This has happened even when our own flour milling industry was down to less than 50 per cent of its capacity. I think we have an obligation, particularly when Canada is making the contribution, to see that the processing is done by Canadians in Canadian mills when Canada is paying for the wheat. I suggest, therefore, that there might be a substantial increase in the amount of flour in our food aid programs. At the present time there is a drop in orders to our Canadian flour mills for export purposes and therefore many men will be laid off very shortly unless additional export orders are secured in time.
In conclusion I should like to say that we think there are some good points in the announcement the minister has made but we

cannot agree, and I am sure the minister himself possibly is not satisfied, that the increase really is in keeping with the increased cost of production.

Mr. Speaker, just before the adjournment I was at the point where I was recommending reform in the expropriation law of Canada. I used as an example my own experience in several cases and one in particular. Before I set out what I recommend should be done I should like to review at this point what does happen so that there will be some chronological order in my address which was interrupted by the statement on motions. At the present time in order to expropriate land for public works, parks or some other purpose, all that is necessary is an order in council passed by a minister. The order in council is filed in the land titles office and it is not necessary that notice be given to the owner of the land which is to be expropriated. The department then moves on to the land unknown to the owner.
In the case I mentioned which went to the Exchequer Court the mineral rights of the C P R. were expropriated for a five year period unknown to the C.P.R. until I brought it to their attention. I had occasion to search the title and found that the C.P.R. had lost all mineral rights. I understand that recently in Banff particularly, where much of this action has taken place under the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing), land was expropriated which recently belonged to the C.P.R. and to other people. The land was returned to the C.P.R. but the land of the other people was not returned to them. Of course there is one law for the C.P.R. and another for the other people in Banff.
What are my recommendations in this regard? In making my recommendations I
May 15, 1967	COMMONS
should like to point out that in this field the crown is all-powerful. The crown decides whether it should take the land. The crown has the money and the power. The crown has the right, the power and the money to hire highly paid appraisers. The crown has the right to do so and hires the most competent lawyers it can obtain. The owner only has his land and in many cases can afford neither an appraiser nor a lawyer.
I have no real criticism of the Exchequer Court as it operates except to say that it really is part of the federal government in the sense of federal jurisdiction. When land is expropriated in Alberta, in Saskatchewan or in other parts of western Canada, it is necessary for the lawyer to come to Ottawa in many cases to present his argument. For example, in the Lake Louise case in which 60 acres were expropriated I had to start proceedings when after a six year period we could not reach a settlement with the government. The crown refused to produce the director of parks for examination for discovery and I had to obtain an order. When the director of parks was produced he refused to answer some questions. I then obtained an order and had to return again to Ottawa.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Under the expropriation law in Canada it can be said truthfully that there is one law for the owner and one for the crown. I say that the jurisdiction in expropriation proceedings should be in the trial division of the Supreme Court of Alberta or in the Queens' Bench, or whatever it may be called, in other provinces. If an agreement cannot be reached between the parties after a specified period of time the onus should fall upon the crown to initiate an action. An individual should not have to commence an action against the crown, as in the famous Fraser case referred to by Mr. Justice Cartwright. Under our laws an individual must commence proceedings and hire appraisers and experts in order to obtain a fair and equitable price for the expropriated land.
I think of a particular case in 1936 where the crown offered to pay $13,000 for a specific piece of property. The owner of that property commenced action and got a judgment for approximately $96,000. I need not say more about that case but I hope what I have said may lead to further consideration on the part of hon. members. My point is that individuals who are the victims of our expropriation laws should not be saddled with the
DEBATES	227
The Address-Mr. Woolliams onus of initiating litigation in order to obtain equity.
Perhaps the attitude of crown agencies in this regard is of benefit to the taxpayers, but I suggest that the crown should pay the initial offer into court and that the owners of the property should be entitled to withdraw that money to pay for the cost of an action initiated to obtain a fair and reasonable price for the property subject to expropriation. I also suggest that in cases where property is expropriated and an action is commenced, which might last for a number of years the crown should be subject to a reasonable interest charge on the original offer during the settlement of such action. The law in this regard should be absolute rather that discretionary in order that the trial judge may assess a 5 or 6 per cent interest rate on the original settlement for expropriation while a determination is being made.
In this regard let me make a special plea to the government, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to look into the whole matter of expropriation in areas such as Banff. There seems to be some difference of opinion as to the legality of expropriation by the crown in respect of lands in national parks under the jurisdiction of the department of northern affairs. I suggest that this whole question should be taken to the Supreme Court of Canada. We have, of course, received opinions from the legal officers of the department of the Minister of Justice, but in any event these actions should be initiated by the crown rather than by private individuals in areas such as Banff and Jasper, Alberta. I might point out that there are other areas in Quebec and Ontario similar to those in western Canada which are subject to the same type of grievous action. There has never been a minister who has occupied the position of the minister of northern affairs who has acted in such a high-handed manner as the present minister in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, like those who preceded me in this debate, I want to express my admiration for the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
COMMONS DEBATES	May 15, 1967
The Address-Mr. Bechard
Those two members, the member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson), through his outstanding eloquence and his truly deep understanding of the current national problems, and the member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote), through his full knowledge of agricultural problems, set the lead, I trust, for the debates to take place in this house in this, our centennial session.
This year, we celebrate the centenary of that historical event which set up, after long deliberations, the framework and the rules within which our country and its citizens have evolved for a century already, while bringing to it the changes necessitated by such circumstances as marked Canadian life since 1867.
So the Canadian people are celebrating this year, with great eclat, that century of coexistence of the two ethnic groups which founded and built together what we know today, with the subsequent contribution of other ethnic groups which came to join the British and the French, and who chose freely to participate in the greatness of the adopted land they cherish and want to see united from coast to coast.
A talk to our new-Canadian fellow-citizens is enough to make us realize very quickly the affection and love they nourish for Canada and their new fellow-countrymen and their great desire to become familiar as soon as possible with one or the other of our two official languages, and sometimes with both.
Surely, all that we admire today, after 100 years, was not always conceived and developed in perfect harmony. Obvious diversities between the two groups, English-speaking and French-speaking, on the cultural, language and traditional levels, are sufficient to explain the frequent clashes of a century of living together.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Let me, Mr. Speaker, be shown a family, whatever the language, the religion or the race, where there is not some difference of opinion! It is perfectly normal. But if certain people, some irresponsible, others with some authority, unceasingly claim that we are celebrating a century of injustice while others, without stating it clearly, hesitate, argue, hem and haw, stand on the fence for demagogic or electioneering purposes, to these people I say they are unfair and dishonest in striking such an attitude. Let it be known that they are not representative of the French Canadian majority opinion, in Quebec and in Canada.

Our language and our religious freedom were guaranteed to us by the 1867 constitution, on the same footing as the English language. Injustices have been committed and will surely be committed again, but should we always blame and accuse our English speaking brothers? Is it their fault if we had such difficulties in finding our place in business, trade and other fields? In certain cases, this is undoubtedly true.
But, Mr. Speaker, let it be explained to me why, at the time of the conquest, our mother country abandoned us? Why did the French financial powers of the time not do to their brethren, whom France had brought to this new and remote land of America and left scattered there, what the British financiers did? Is it any fault of the latter?
In spite of such desertion, which I might even call treason, the French Canadian people, determined to survive, overcame every difficulty and every obstacle. They gave themselves institutions of high learning to train our clergy, our political men, our businessmen, our industrialists of whom many made and continue to make their mark in this country, thus contributing to the economic progress of Canada. Less than ten years ago, Quebec, tired of marking time, thanks to a people willing and determined to assume its proper place and to improve its economic, cultural and social condition, thanks to the alert mind of an elite and thanks also to the arrival on the local political scenes of dynamic leaders, Quebec became increasingly aware of its problems and of the role it should play within confederation. A new impetus was given to education, our economy and our federal-provincial relations. It was an almost complete transformation in every field, and thus an awakening, perhaps belated, but how thrilling, for a population accustomed to the drab routine of laissez jaire and traditional inertia.
That new awakening of Quebec upset a number of people, namely the Quebec people, and their determination to contribute more and more to the administration of the country, Canada, disturbed the peaceful life of more than one of our English-speaking brothers who felt panic in the face of that clear stand and fear of losing their place.
Mr. Speaker, the people of Quebec do not want to supplant anyone. They do not want to take anyone's place; far from it. What they want is to take their place, that which belongs
May 15. 1967	COMMONS
to them, as there is one for their Englishspeaking brothers, in their country's administration. They want to take a greater part in the economic, social, cultural and political development of their country and, to that effect, thay want not only to be heard but to be understood when they talk and write their own language, one of the country's two official languages. The people of Quebec do not want to separate and they do not want a separate status such as some politicians looking for publicity and votes are now advocating in Quebec and which would be equivalent to separation. What they want is to be respected and understood when they speak to the administrators of their country in their own language and above all, to live decently, have a job and earn a sufficient income to meet their obligations, as well as to be fairly well off to avoid falling prey to communism, a constant menace to the world, that poverty and destitution, so exploited by unscrupulous demagogues, can foster in our country. Communist propagandists always make the most of disagreements and crises of all types to spread their beliefs.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has fully understood the legitimate demands of the Quebec people for equal opportunities.
That is why, since 1963, the policy of the present government has tended to create a situation more favourable to the development of the country and of bilingualism, particularly within the public service, and to provide equal participation and advancement opportunities for French Canadians and secure for them the status of first class citizens in Canada.
If that is not working for national unity, Mr. Speaker, we must ask ourselves what concept of unity have those who are always talking nonsense of the kind we again heard in this house recently from the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who follows the example set by his leader and many others.
It is obvious that he does not understand the problem of unity in the slightest and that he has not yet asked himself the question: What does Quebec want?
Referring to the member for Yukon, he would have done better, after three or four short appearances in this house, since October 5, 1966, busy as he was, I suppose, collecting material for scandals so as to better play his role of character assassination with his accomplices who are just like him, he would have done better to refrain from destroying, by his ridicule, everything positive achieved 27053-16
DEBATES	229
The Address-Mr. Bechard by the Prime Minister and his government since 1963, and rouse feelings that were dying out.
You only have to travel through our vast country and speak with our fellow-citizens, whatever their origin, to notice the tremendous evolution which has occurred in the direction of the principle adopted by our present leader of the government confronted by the consciousness of Quebecers since 1960.
Mr. Speaker, in the time allotted to me, I cannot deal in detail with all the proposals contained in the speech from the throne. However, I should like to discuss briefly a very delicate and controversial matter: television and radio broadcasting. I will conclude my remarks by speaking of the dairy industry in Canada, particularly in the Gaspe peninsula, adding some comments on other matters of local nature, but considered very important for the riding of Bonaventure in particular.
The speech from the throne had this to say concerning television and radio broadcasting:
Recognizing that broadcasting is an important cultural instrument, the government supports a comprehensive and balanced national broadcasting service-
I have already made my position clear to the house concerning the quality of certain programs shown particularly on television.
I do not have to take back a word of the speech which I delivered in this house, as recorded in Hansard of February 25, 1964, except the reference to a greater state control. After the affair of "This Hour Has Seven Days", when the matter of internal control was publicly discussed, endangering the basic authority of that institution, I said that a direct control and intervention of the government in those matters of administration and programming in and out of season would turn that state corporation into a weak instrument in the hands of the government, whatever the party in power, which I could not accept.
However, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is highly important to establish a well-defined authority in the hands of management and to empower the latter to exercise such authority efficiently and advisedly.
The producers should be shown that bad taste and displays of immorality have no place in public, in a civilized country. Let us have an opportunity, from time to time, to make a clean sweep of these free-thinkers, who, under the cover of freedom of speech, use the state networks and others to distil drop by drop the ferment of revolution and subversive
May IS, 1967

The Address-Mr. Bechard ideologies which are unacceptable in a free democratic country-and here it must be understood that freedom does not mean licence.
Radio and television are too valuable information and culture media to be used too often, in my view, to infect our population. I hope that the new legislation will see that a body such as the board of governors, for instance, is granted the necessary power to prevent any excessive abuse of airwaves, as is unfortunately too often the case.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The farm policy which was the subject of a subamendment moved last Friday by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) was officially announced in the house by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) on March 22 last for the dairy year 1967-68. It will be recalled that farm and dairy producer organizations asked for $5.10 per hundredweight of milk. The policy announced by the government set that price at $4.75. When the terms of that policy were published by the Canadian Dairy Commission, quick response arose from professional farming quarters.
Attempts were first made, in certain circles to intimate that the farmers were overdoing it and that they had no cause to fear that they could not receive the national average price of $4.75 per hundredweight. For some areas, where the dairy industry is very well set up from production to processing and marketing, I would agree that such an argument might be true, but for an area such as Bonaventure and other less advanced areas where the number of dairy producers is less than a thousand with about 40 per cent having to look elsewhere for a supplementary income, those claims are fair and legitimate.
Some will say that the government policy is intended to develop an efficient and healthy dairy industry in Canada mainly through the expansion of dairy farms.
I am all for it, because in my opinion we cannot expect some day the dairy farmer for instance to go on his own, if his unit is not economical, which means sufficient cultivated land, a quality herd with a sufficient number of milk cows, adequate equipment and plant facilities, a market for his dairy products, if certain farms, which have never assured a decent income to their owners are kept in operation by maintaining the present system. For some dairy farms, a $20 subsidy per hundredweight would not even be adequate.
However, taking into consideration what was mentioned earlier with regard to my area


of Bonaventure, the manufacturer at the processing plant will not be able to pay this year, on the basis of last year's production on which the quota will be established, more than $2.94 per hundredweight. Add $1.21 to that, less the 11 per cent premium for exports, and you get a total of $4.04 per hundredweight. That is a far cry from $4.75 per hundredweight, although it is much better than the corresponding figure for last year. The quota policy, although well inspired, took many by surprise. In my area, particularly, it certainly does not encourage consolidation of farms or the expansion of our dairy farms.
Indeed, the farmer who last year gradually added a few cattle to his dairy herd, will not be able to benefit from the resulting additional production this year, if I understand correctly the data of the Canadian Dairy Commission.
I therefore ask the Minister of Agriculture to study seriously this whole question of quotas, with a view to modifying it in such a way that dairy producers in our area, as in many others, might hope to become more efficient and capable of earning a decent income. That is all the dairy producer wants, and only that.
On the other hand, I would like to remind the house that the assurance that the farmer will be paid the specified amount of $3.54 per hundredweight of milk by the plant can only come from the provincial government, which is the only body able to legislate in this matter.
Ontario did it, and the Quebec government, with its department of agriculture headed by a man who left his mark by his criticism of the federal Department of Agriculture, should act without delay. In this way, the Gaspe farmer too could derive greater profit from the generous policy of the federal government.
A vote in favour of the subamendment of the hon. member for Roberval tonight, Mr. Speaker, would not mean $5.10 per hundredweight, but could result, if the government were defeated, in an expense of some $18 to $20 million for Canadian taxpayers, an amount which I suggest could be put to better use.
I will now address my remarks to the minister responsible for the implementation of public works which are of great importance for us in the riding of Bonaventure. As matter of fact, harbour facilities are needed by the fishermen as well as by the present industries
May 15, 1967

and the ones to come, and that means building new facilities as well as repairing the existing ones.
Important works just begun at Paspebiac were made necessary by the recent development of the fishing industry.
On the other hand, in the fall of 1965, after many representations, I secured the lengthening of the wharf at Carleton from where about forty million feet of lumber are shipped each year. The traffic is heavy from April to January.
Now, that work has been left in abeyance in the spring of 1966 because the department considered it unacceptable. Since then, after every conceivable recrimination, nothing is being done to correct that situation and the wharf is in such an alarming state of disrepair that I am now wondering whether it would not be better to build a new one. Those who use the wharf, the municipal authorities and others, are constantly making representations to me and I am wondering why certain people are so slow in requiring immediate action on the part of the contractor. Such a situation has lasted too long and it is urgent to put an end to all this red tape.
My riding being located almost entirely along the Baie des Chaleurs, properties are therefore constantly threatened by the normal erosion of the sea, and sometimes storms like the one we had in late December 1966, the worst in thirty years, cause damage that owners are financially unable to repair. Up to 1956, the federal government allotted a certain amount to make good such damages, but since then, thanks to their ingeniousness, certain officials were able to convince the then minister to replace such a policy by the famous "federal responsibility when erosion is caused by navigation or the presence of a federal structure". Certain properties are gradually disappearing hopelessly. During a storm last December, several properties in St. Omer, Carleton, Maria, New Richmond, Cap-lan, St. Simeon and all along the coast, were seriously damaged; I call for the special attention of the government for the immediate construction of retaining walls.
Means of transportation are for our area, far as it is, Mr. Speaker, of the utmost importance. In this atomic age, our area is deprived of air service of any kind. A daily service would perhaps not be economic, but so long as there has been no experimentation in this field, that will be impossible to prove. A Gaspe company-Air Gaspe-is operating a
The Address-Mr. Bechard service between Gaspe, the Magdalen Islands, Ste-Anne-des-Monts and the north coast. Let the Minister of Transport help it to operate the service between Gaspe and Quebec, via Bonaventure, of course, where an airport belonging to the provincial government could, I think, be bought easily, and Gaspe will then welcome with enthusiasm and relief an innovation made necessary by the need to connect us to the great centres in the country.
During the last few years, the public organizations in Gaspe and the members from the south coast of the province, speaking on behalf of the population, have been asking the C.N.R. for a passenger train operating directly between Montreal and Gaspe.
Now, it so happened that last March, the authorities of the C.N.R. finally agreed to our request and on May 31, 1967, the new era of a direct train from Montreal to Gaspe will begin. At this point, I want to thank all the public bodies as well as the Canadian National Railways for their co-operation and the Minister of Transport for his efficient participation in the final success of our efforts to this end. However, as was to be expected, once again Gaspe could not count on complete enjoyment or achievement. In fact, we are informed that the "Chaleur", upon arrival at Matapedia, at the junction of the Maritimes and Gaspe lines, the trains will not immediately start on the Gaspe run, but will have to go to Campbellton, New Brunswick, at least 13 miles away to be cleaned, serviced, fueled, etc., and return to Matapedia before going on to Gaspe. This shuttling, plus service time, means about an hour and a naif, very conservatively.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the people of Bonaventure riding and Gaspe and the travelling public in general cannot accept these early-morning and night-time side trips into a neighbouring province. We do not accept it and we shall not accept it.
The argument is that this situation is temporary; we are afraid of these temporary situations which suddenly and ordinarily become permanent. We see the trap and we refuse to fall into it.
Further, if we look at the train schedule recently published by the C.N.R., to be in force from April 30 to October 28, 1967, we are surprised to note that the "Chaleur" will make only 14 stops on the Matapedia-Gaspe run as against 32 by the present self-propelled coach. A matter of saving time, I will be told. In such a case, why lose from an hour and a half to two hours, morning and night, to go to
232	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Bechard Campbellton? The trap becomes increasingly evident.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
But that is not all. The rate we will have to pay for the so-called favours of the C.N.R. is even higher. Trains Nos. 245 and 246 will be eliminated May 31, 1967, according to the previously mentioned schedule. On these freight and express trains, a coach was attached to serve passengers unable to use the self-propelled coach. All this will be eliminated on May 31, thus depriving many employees of their livelihood. And this, Mr. Speaker, has been decided upon without any consultation with the Gaspe population, by a decision of the C.N.R. authorities.
The people of Bonaventure riding and Gaspe will not be fooled this way. The population is now warned and constantly alerted.
Consequently, I urge the authorities of the Canadian National Railways to reconsider their decision and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) to use his influence and good offices once more to persuade the Canadian National authorities to correct those deplorable errors without delay, before May 31, 1967. The service of the "Chaleur" can very well be done at Matapedia or elsewhere along the line, which will make unnecessary that intriguing eventual pilgrim to our New Brunswick neighbours and will really give satisfaction to the travelling public.
I would have many other subjects to deal with tonight, Mr. Speaker, but in view of the passage of time, I will reserve for other occasions the pleasure of doing so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in participating in this debate for the next few minutes I should like first of all to join those who have offered their congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
There are a number of serious problems in my own constituency, Mr. Speaker, to which I intend to draw the attention of the house. I had intended to make a rather lengthy and detailed speech respecting wheat prices and wheat marketing in western Canada. As you know, and as other hon. members know, within the last hour we have had an announcement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) respecting this matter. We realize it is not easy in negotiations with other countries for the representatives of any country to get all they feel they need for the people they represent.
The 21-cent increase in the maximum price over the next three years certainly does not constitute a reasonable increase in keeping with the increased cost of producing wheat. For example, I have in front of me a brief prepared by a committee in my constituency. This brief was taken to a lot of meetings throughout the constituency and presented to the farmers to find out whether or not there was a measure of agreement with respect to what the current selling price of wheat ought to be. After much consideration the very reasonable people in the farm community decided that to keep pace with the increased cost of production during the last three years there was now justification for demanding not less than $2.75 a bushel to the farmer. This is substantially more than the amount suggested by the Minister of Trade and Commerce today. I know the minister agrees that if an increase in the selling price of wheat were made in direct proportion to the increased cost of production, then $2.75 in 1967 would not be an unreasonable figure.
This group of farmers in my constituency addressed a brief to me and in the resume of their brief they asked me to support their request for a two-price system for the sale of wheat of at least $2.75 per bushel for the first 4,000 bushels sold by each farmer and then whatever can be obtained on the international market for wheat sold in excess of 4,000 bushels. They give these reasons for their demands:
1.	The rising costs of farm operations.
May IS, 1967

This is well known to members of this house and everyone else who is at all familiar with the farm community today.
2.	Competing incomes of those in industry to the incomes of farmers.
3.	Departure of farmers from farms to positions m industry.
4.	Impending food shortages in Canada and in the world.
I am not sure I can agree that there is an impending shortage of wheat in Canada but there certainly appears to be an impending shortage of foodstuffs available for people throughout the world. Therefore the announcement this evening, with respect to the future price of wheat, while it represents a slight upward adjustment, certainly is not in keeping with the rising costs.
All the other negotiations between the signatory countries to the international wheat agreement were carried on in a situation where there was a huge surplus of wheat, particularly on the North American continent. In 1960 and again in 1963 and 1964 there were huge surpluses of wheat in the United States and Canada which had been carried over from year to year. I suggest that in this kind of situation it is reasonably easy for the purchasing countries to demand that there be no increase or in some cases that the maximum price be decreased. In that kind of situation, when we are trying to sell against continuing surpluses from one year to the next, it is rather difficult for the Canadian negotiators to convince the purchasers there should be an increase in price. However, in 1967 there are no huge surpluses left.
Over the years the farmers have accepted the argument advanced that it was difficult to get an increase in price as long as we were producing far in excess of current market demands. This situation has changed. There are no longer any huge surpluses of wheat in the United States. After Canada has fulfilled all the commitments under the agreements that we have made to date there will be no huge surpluses left in Canada either. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, had it not been for the substantially larger than ordinary crops in western Canada during these last three years we would be unable to meet the commitments we have made to date. Last year wheat production in Canada amounted to over 800 million bushels, a record far above the production level of any previous year. The year before we had a record-breaking crop of over 700 million bushels. But the demand for food, and particularly for wheat, has gone up to the
The Address-Mr. Olson point where these surpluses no longer exist. Surely, this fact should have been taken into account. I am not going to spend a great deal more time on that subject this evening because I am sure that as this session progresses there will be other opportunities to discuss the matter of a just and reasonable price for wheat.
I want to turn now for a moment to the matter of the very severe snowstorms we have had in southern Alberta during the last two or three weeks. I spent a number of days in that part of my constituency which was most severely affected by these storms. The situation is tragic. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) came out and after listening to some of the ranchers and farmers in the area termed it a national disaster. It is difficult to believe until you see it. In southern Alberta, where spring usually arrives about the middle of March, we have had as much as 70 to 100 inches of snow. The snow actually reached the point where it halted surface traffic regardless of the kind of equipment used. The snowplows were unable to cope with the heavy, wet snow.
In many parts of southern Alberta heavy bulldozers had to be brought in to break trails to bring food to livestock stranded on the summer pastures. Even this equipment found difficulty in opening trails. The emergency measures organization in Alberta was able to obtain the assistance of a number of helicopters. While they could not move in sufficient food to keep all the animals from starving in these isolated places, they certainly were a great help. We should recognize the tremendous advantage of having an emergency measures organization which can move quickly to give the kind of assistance which was required in southern Alberta during these very trying three weeks.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I also think we should pay tribute to the United States Air Force. They were asked if they had any helicopters in the area, I believe on a Sunday, at a time when it became apparent that emergency action would have to be taken. Through the United States consulate in Edmonton, and I presume also through Ottawa, in a very few hours two large helicopters were sent from one of the air force bases in Montana. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, they were first on the scene. This kind of co-operation and rendering of immediate assistance in response to a request for machines in the area is something for

May 15. 1967
The Address-Mr. Olson which we Canadians should be grateful. We should be grateful that we are living alongside a neighbour who responds so quickly to this sort of request.
We also owe a great debt of gratitude for the co-operation received from all of the municipalities to the north of where the storm struck. For example, the city of Calgary dispatched a train loaded with snow removal equipment to the city of Lethbridge to assist the city in digging itself out of what was an almost impossible situation and far beyond the capacity of the city of Lethbridge to cope with the machinery that was there.
Mention has been made of livestock losses. One press report that I saw indicated that some 15,000 head of cattle in southern Alberta may have been lost. I have in front of me the Lethbridge Herald for May 12, some days later, in which it is estimated that there may be a total of as many as 40,000 baby calf losses. In addition there will be losses of growing cattle from starvation and for other reasons.
I was in this area for several days, and even the estimate of 40,000 new calves which died is far too low. I visited a number of ranches where the loss of baby calves was anywhere from 20 per cent to as high as 90 per cent of the total number of calves expected. This will far exceed the estimate of 40,000 when we realize that there are something like 200,000 head of female stock in the area that was affected.
This is a disaster of the highest level for some of the individuals involved. First of all, it means that for some there will be no income for 1967. Some people have lost anywhere from 25 to 30 per cent of their calf crop, which represents whatever profit they would have had after deduction of expenses for the year. Perhaps they can survive, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps they can get along with What other crops they may grow. But there are others who will be virtually put out of business because of this storm. They lost not only almost their entire calf crop for 1967 but also a large percentage of the breeding stock on the farms and ranches.
The Minister of Agriculture visited the area and suggested that the federal government stood ready to give short-term assistance in paying for the cost of moving feed. This involved the use of some of this high priced equipment such as helicopters and snow equipment. The minister also said there would be some long-term assistance for those

who were hit hardest. By that I presume he means the ones who are virtually out of the livestock business because of their losses.
In this regard we should like to know fairly soon what the minister has in mind. Does he simply mean that some credit will be made available to enable these people to purchase new breeding stock? Is some compensation to be paid those who suffered the greatest loss? If so, what kind of program will be set up to make compensation available to those who qualify? We do not know. We know that the minister termed it a national disaster, and having witnessed the scene I know that this is true in the case of many individuals. But, Mr. Speaker, I am apprehensive about statements of this sort, and with good reason.
It is only two or three years ago that a very serious situation developed in the Peace River country of northern Alberta where a large group of farmers had been completely without income and without crops for a period of three years. That to them was also a disaster. Federal ministers and officials visited the scene, made a survey and then announced to the press that they stood ready to be of assistance. Following this the provincial government went ahead and instituted a program to offer some assistance to the farmers in this area who had had crop failures during this three-year period.
When it came to the federal government paying its share, which had been worked out on a 50-50 basis between the two levels of government, it did not come through with the money. I do not want to be difficult or unfair, but a letter was sent by the federal Minister of Agriculture at that time to the provincial minister of agriculture in connection with these fanners in the Peace River area to the effect that the federal government would share on a 50-50 basis in whatever kind of assistance program the province set up. After the program was set up and the farmers were given an indication of the type of assistance which would be given to them to purchase seed and make arrangements to meet the expense of sowing another crop, the federal government advised the province that it would not participate, that the farmers should have had crop insurance, that they should put the area under a crop insurance scheme so that they would not face this situation in future.
I see from the clock that you -will shortly be interrupting the debate so we may vote, Mr. Speaker, so in closing I want to say that we hope the federal Minister of Agriculture
May 15. 1967

was serious when	he said that the govemment stood ready	to offer all reasonable assistance, both short term and long term, to prevent the collapse of some of the farming and ranching units. We will be looking forward to his coming up with a program and	
we hope he will	keep these commitments
when it comes to the practical application of a reasonable assistance program.
